extraction.body: Security researcher Dor Zvi and his team at the cybersecurity firm he cofounded, RedAccess, analyzed thousands of vibe-coded web applications created using the AI software development tools Lovable, Replit, Base44, and Netlify and found more than 5,000 of them that had virtually no security or authentication of any kind. Many of these web apps allowed anyone who merely finds their web URL to access the apps and their data. Around 40 percent of the apps exposed sensitive data, Zvi says, including medical information, financial data, corporate presentations, and strategy documents, as well as detailed logs of customer conversations with chatbots. “The end result is that organizations are actually leaking private data through vibe-coding applications,” says Zvi. “This is one of the biggest events ever where people are exposing corporate or other sensitive information to anyone in the world.” Zvi says RedAccess’ scouring for vulnerable web apps was surprisingly easy. Lovable, Replit, Base44, and Netlify all allow users to host their web apps on those AI companies' own domains, rather than the users’. So the researchers used straightforward Google and Bing searches for those AI companies' domains combined with other search terms to identify thousands of apps that had been vibe coded with the companies' tools. Of the 5,000 AI-coded apps that Zvi says were left publicly accessible to anyone who simply typed their URLs into a browser, he found close to 2,000 that, upon closer inspection, seemed to reveal private data: Screenshots of web apps he shared with WIRED—several of which WIRED verified were still online and exposed—showed what appeared to be a hospital's work assignments with the personally identifiable information of doctors, a company's detailed ad purchasing information, what appeared to be another firm's go-to-market strategy presentation, a retailer's full logs of its chatbot's conversations with customers, including the customers' full names and contact information, a shipping firm's cargo records, and assorted sales and financial records from a variety of other companies. In some cases, Zvi says, he found that the exposed apps would have allowed him to gain administrative privileges over systems and even remove other administrators. In the case of Lovable, Zvi says he also found numerous examples of phishing sites that impersonated major corporations, including Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe’s, and McDonald’s, that appeared to have been created with the AI coding tool and hosted on Lovable's domain. When WIRED asked the four AI coding companies about RedAccess’ findings, Netlify didn’t respond, but the three other companies pushed back on the researchers’ claims and protested that they hadn't shared enough of their findings or provided enough time for them to respond. (RedAccess says it reached out to the companies on Monday.) But they didn't deny that the web apps RedAccess found were left exposed. “From the limited information they shared, [RedAccess's] core claim appears to be that some users have published apps on the open web that should’ve been private,” Replit's CEO Amjad Masad wrote in a response post on X. “Replit allows users to choose whether apps are public or private. Public apps being accessible on the internet is expected behavior. Privacy settings can be changed at any time with a single click.” A spokesperson for Lovable responded in a statement that “Lovable takes reports of exposed data and phishing sites seriously, and we're actively working to obtain what we need to investigate. It's also worth noting that Lovable gives builders the tools to build securely, but how an app is configured is ultimately the creator's responsibility.” Blake Brodie, the head of public relations for Base44's parent company, Wix, wrote in a statement that “Base44 provides users with robust tools to configure their own applications' security, including access controls and visibility settings.” She added that “disabling those controls is a deliberate, straightforward action, any user can do it. Where applications were publicly accessible, that reflects a user configuration choice, not a platform vulnerability.” Brodie also noted that “it is trivially easy to fabricate applications that appear to contain real user data. Without a single verified example provided to us, we have no way to assess the validity of these claims.” RedAccess, for its part, disputed that it hadn't provided examples to Base44. Zvi notes that for a few dozen exposed web apps, it went so far as to contact the app's apparent owner, which confirmed that data had been exposed. RedAccess also shared with WIRED anonymized communications in several cases that showed Base44 users thanking the researchers for alerting them to exposed web apps, which were then secured or taken offline. Verifying whether real data has been exposed on any particular unsecured AI-coded web app can be tricky, says Joel Margolis, a security researcher who, along with a colleague, recently discovered that an AI chat toy had exposed 50,000 conversations the toy had with children on a website with virtually no security. Data in a vibe-coded web app might be a placeholder, he says, or the app might be just a proof of concept. Wix’s Brodie argued that two examples that WIRED shared with Base44 did appear to be test sites or have AI-generated data. For the web apps WIRED reviewed, we couldn't confirm that the personal or corporate data was as sensitive—or real—as it appeared to be. Margolis nonetheless says that the problem of AI-built web apps exposing data is very real. “Somebody from a marketing team wants to create a website. And unless you ask them to do it securely, they're not going to go out of their way to do that.” Zvi points out that the 5,000 exposed apps Red Access found were only those hosted on the AI coding tools' own domains, and that likely thousands more are hosted on users' own purchased domains. He compares the ongoing deluge of data exposures that are resulting from companies' unsecured AI-coded web apps to the epidemic of exposed data created by the security settings of Amazon S3 storage buckets in earlier years. Companies from Verizon to World Wrestling Entertainment accidentally exposed reams of sensitive data due to misconfigurations in their instance of Amazon's cloud storage service. AI web-app coding tools are now creating a wave of data exposures, the result of a similar combination of user error and lack of safeguards, Zvi says. Yet more fundamental than any particular security failing on the part of the AI coding companies, he argues, is simply that these tools allow a new class of people within organizations to create applications—often with little security awareness and outside the usual software development processes that companies use to vet applications before they're released. “Anyone from your company at any moment can generate an app, and this is not going through any development cycle or any security check,” Zvi says. “People can just start using it in production without asking anyone.

sources.title: Google lets you make personal Android apps for free now – with just prompts - ZDNET
passages: Are you tired of ad overload in free, single-task apps?
Or, can you not find an app that fits a weirdly specific need?
Now you can make custom apps for your own Android phone, even if you have zero coding experience.

You’ll be able to share your apps with close family and friends in the coming months, but you don’t have to.
Custom Android apps make app development a much more personal and potentially user-friendly experience.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android It just got a whole lot easier to vibe code the exact Android app you need - no developer experience required. Are you tired of ad overload in free, single-task apps? Or, can you not find an app that fits a weirdly specific need? Now you can make custom apps for your own Android phone, even if you have zero coding experience. One Tuesday, Google announced that anyone with a standard Google account can build personal apps in Google AI Studio. These apps will run on your own device, launched from a private part of Google Play, and won’t be included in the public Play Store. Also: ‘What’s your AI stack?’ The new job interview question you need to answer You’ll be able to share your apps with close family and friends in the coming months, but you don’t have to. If you do share an app you create and it takes off, Google will provide a “pipeline to graduate into a professional developer account,” meaning you’ll be able to share your app globally via the Play Store. To get started, access the tool in Google AI Studio . There is an app creator in AI Studio, but that’s intended for professional developer accounts and requires USB debugging connected to a PC. This new tool works with that same creator, but it lets you install your app on a personal device with a single click and later directly share it instead of utilizing a public Play Store listing. In the tool, you describe what you want in a prompt, and AI does the rest. While the app is under creation, you’ll see options to add features you might have missed. You can make light edits once the app is complete, or you can completely scrap it and start again. There’s no charge to experiment and build an app. Custom Android apps make app development a much more personal and potentially user-friendly experience. It could be a fantastic option for replacing apps on your phone that you only use for a single thing – like a habit tracker, a calculator or converter, or a specific counter or timer. The ability to make an app with AI isn’t new, but the big selling point here is that you can make an app completely for yourself . Also: I used a free, open-source AI tool to build a working app – in two days My wife had surgery recently, and part of her recovery involves an array of specifically timed medicines, supplements, and liquids. She downloaded a simple tracker app to stay on top of things, but the app was loaded with ads to the point it was too frustrating to use. A monthly subscription was offered to nix the ads, but she didn’t want to pay for an app that would only be used for a few months. Searching for similar apps yielded similar results. With Google’s new system, it seems like it would be simple to make a custom app that avoids both the ads and the fees. And even better, you can tailor this app specifically to what you need. Perhaps the best part about this system is that an app you make doesn’t have to be commercially viable, and it doesn’t even have to be an app that anyone else needs. It just has to work for you . extraction.body: Google plans to help turn those personal AI-generated apps into wide releases. Google has already added a few AI features to the Play Store, but a lot more are coming . The previously released Ask Play feature is expanding to offer more AI-powered discovery options in Google’s app store, and Google is also using AI to build a recommendation engine called Game Finder. For people who have embraced AI to build their own apps, the Play Store will soon offer a way to privately host and share those creations. Google rolled out Ask Play in 2025 as a small chatbot interface on Play Store listings. It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries. Starting today, Ask Play is expanding into a more general way to search for apps and games. You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts. Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon. Google’s other AI discovery announcement focuses on games. The new Game Finder feature leans on all the usage data Google’s app platform has hoovered up over the years, featuring insights into the way 1.2 billion people play games on Android. It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA. You can tune your DNA profile by rating the games you’ve played, which supposedly leads to more accurate recommendations. There will be game playlists to peruse, along with various contextual lists like relaxing, trending titles, and more specific lists based on mechanics you’ve seen in previous games. Game Finder also lets you add or remove tags to further adjust the games Google’s AI suggests. Google says you’ll eventually be able to prompt Game Finder with fairly specific game preferences, but it’s unclear how much customization will be available at launch. Game Finder and Gamer DNA are rolling out in the US today, with other markets following “soon.” Despite its slow progress in coding-focused AI models lately, Google is continuing to push this as a core feature of its products. Anyone who has been tinkering with vibe-coded apps in AI Studio will soon have a direct pipe into the Play Store. This is not the same as publishing an app as a developer, but that could be the end result. There won’t be any tedious downloading of APK files or tinkering with a developer console—you’ll be able to send apps to the Play Store right from AI Studio. Adding a vibe coded app to the Play Store creates a “Personal Library” accessible from the app store client on your device. This is available only to you by default, providing an easy way to install and manage the apps via Google’s system. Google says you can share these apps with “a small group” of friends and family. Google has not decided how many people count as a small group yet, but this type of distribution doesn’t require a developer account. If you want to share beyond that, Google plans to have an onboarding process to set you up with a developer profile to publish your vibe coded apps. If you do this, you’ll be subject to the same app review guidelines as developers who come into Google Play in the traditional way. Private apps are not reviewed by Google. Private vibe-coded apps in the Play Store will begin rolling out today in the US and select other markets. The private-to-public app migration option will be available in the coming months. It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries. Starting today, Ask Play is expanding into a more general way to search for apps and games. You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts. Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon.

Google’s other AI discovery announcement focuses on games. The new Game Finder feature leans on all the usage data Google’s app platform has hoovered up over the years, featuring insights into the way 1.2 billion people play games on Android. It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA.

You can tune your DNA profile by rating the games you’ve played, which supposedly leads to more accurate recommendations. There will be game playlists to peruse, along with various contextual lists like relaxing, trending titles, and more specific lists based on mechanics you’ve seen in previous games. Game Finder also lets you add or remove tags to further adjust the games Google’s AI suggests. Google says you’ll eventually be able to prompt Game Finder with fairly specific game preferences, but it’s unclear how much customization will be available at launch. Game Finder and Gamer DNA are rolling out in the US today, with other markets following “soon.”

Despite its slow progress in coding-focused AI models lately, Google is continuing to push this as a core feature of its products. Anyone who has been tinkering with vibe-coded apps in AI Studio will soon have a direct pipe into the Play Store. This is not the same as publishing an app as a developer, but that could be the end result.

There won’t be any tedious downloading of APK files or tinkering with a developer console—you’ll be able to send apps to the Play Store right from AI Studio. Adding a vibe coded app to the Play Store creates a “Personal Library” accessible from the app store client on your device. This is available only to you by default, providing an easy way to install and manage the apps via Google’s system.

Google says you can share these apps with “a small group” of friends and family. Google has not decided how many people count as a small group yet, but this type of distribution doesn’t require a developer account. If you want to share beyond that, Google plans to have an onboarding process to set you up with a developer profile to publish your vibe coded apps. If you do this, you’ll be subject to the same app review guidelines as developers who come into Google Play in the traditional way. Private apps are not reviewed by Google.
Private vibe-coded apps in the Play Store will begin rolling out today in the US and select other markets. The private-to-public app migration option will be available in the coming months.

With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

passages: I found an app called Hotkeys that seemed to do what I wanted, but it left the App Store quite a while ago, presumably because it was designed for Intel-based hardware. (Apple is ending support for such apps with macOS 28.) You May Also Like But now that Golden Gate has deeper Apple Intelligence tools, I decided to use Claude Code and Xcode to vibe code a modern, intuitive, and unobtrusive hotkey app called KeyRun.
You can tell Claude not to waste tokens by complimenting you, but even an AI agent’s praise is good to have, so I didn't.
I also had Claude build a “save” feature that saves a set of keyboard shortcuts to a file, so that I could copy the file to another system and use the same hotkeys.

extraction.body: I've always wanted a straightforward way to launch apps, open documents in their default apps, or bring up folders on macOS via hotkeys. To do the same in macOS, you either have to build a multistep process via the Shortcuts app or download a third-party utility such as FastScripts 3 , HomeRow , Karabiner-Elements , Keyboard Maestro , or Raycast . These apps and others that I've tried work, but they are either unnecessarily complex or cost more than I want to spend. I found an app called Hotkeys that seemed to do what I wanted, but it left the App Store quite a while ago, presumably because it was designed for Intel-based hardware. (Apple is ending support for such apps with macOS 28.) You May Also Like But now that Golden Gate has deeper Apple Intelligence tools, I decided to use Claude Code and Xcode to vibe code a modern, intuitive, and unobtrusive hotkey app called KeyRun. And, of course, I made it free for anyone to download from the Mac App Store. Setting Up the AI Workbench in macOS Golden Gate Apple’s Xcode programming app already had AI integrations in macOS Sequoia , but the connections are tighter in the Golden Gate beta. For one, your conversations now take place in the main Xcode window rather than in a sidebar. Installing Claude (Credit: Apple/PCMag) To get started, you’ll need a Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini chatbot account. Then, in Xcode, simply go to Settings > Intelligence and click Get next to the agent you want to install. I chose Claude and got right into prompting . Prompting KeyRun to Life—and Bypassing Mac's Permissions Trap I began by asking Claude, “Can you create a simple, intuitive macOS app that assigns hotkeys to applications, so that I can submit it to the App Store? I want the app to create a hotkey for any app that I either drag into the app’s window or choose from a list of files.” Claude complied, and in a few seconds, it coded an app that matched my specifications. I was able to view the actual code by opening its files from the Xcode sidebar. I then asked Claude to rewrite the app so that it wouldn’t create hotkeys that macOS already uses , such as Cmd-Q (quit the current app) or Cmd-S (save the current document). It agreed to this and subsequently made the app check any new shortcuts against the list of system-wide hotkeys that macOS maintains in the background. Coding with Claude (Credit: Apple/PCMag) But then I hit a complication. When I tried to use a hotkey I had created, macOS told me I needed to grant it Accessibility permission in the System Settings app. I didn’t want prospective users to deal with this annoyance, so I asked Claude if a workaround was possible. Claude immediately solved the problem by rewriting the app’s hotkey mechanism to use Apple’s ancient Carbon framework instead of the modern AppKit’s global event monitor. Apple officially states that Carbon, in general, is deprecated, but it never explicitly got rid of the Carbon hotkey mechanism and has even updated it for 64-bit macOS environments. Almost all existing hotkey apps use this mechanism, so it's not likely to go away anytime soon. At this point, Claude suggested that we save the project and give it a name. Claude, sounding like a restaurant waiter who says “Excellent Choice!” no matter what you choose from the menu, told me it was an excellent name. You can tell Claude not to waste tokens by complimenting you, but even an AI agent’s praise is good to have, so I didn't. Then, I got ambitious and asked Claude to add a feature that could open documents, not only apps, from a hotkey. Claude did exactly that, adding the detail that it would add only those documents that normally open in a default app when you double-click on them. I pushed things further by asking for an option to open folders with hotkeys. Every time Claude added a feature, I thought of another. I also had Claude build a “save” feature that saves a set of keyboard shortcuts to a file, so that I could copy the file to another system and use the same hotkeys. After that, I had Claude add profiles so I could use a different set of hotkeys when working on documents and editing images. Finally, I asked Claude to create a hotkey for KeyRun itself. KeyRun app interface (Credit: Ed Mendelson/PCMag) At every stage, Claude and I consulted on which keyboard shortcuts to use in the app’s menus for each new feature. Claude suggested that the app should automatically delete the hotkey assignment if it couldn’t find the app or document associated with it, but I reminded Claude that the user might decide to bring back the app or document, and that the user should be able to decide whether to keep or delete an obsolete hotkey assignment—and Claude agreed. The last thing I did was add an option to launch KeyRun automatically upon startup. Surviving the App Store Review: Beta Bugs and Rejections When the app seemed complete, I asked Claude to guide me through submitting it to the Mac App Store. Of course, if you want to create an app just for personal needs, you can skip these steps.

And unless you ask them to do it securely, they're not going to go out of their way to do that.” Zvi points out that the 5,000 exposed apps Red Access found were only those hosted on the AI coding tools' own domains, and that likely thousands more are hosted on users' own purchased domains.

Around 40 percent of the apps exposed sensitive data, Zvi says, including medical information, financial data, corporate presentations, and strategy documents, as well as detailed logs of customer conversations with chatbots.
Data in a vibe-coded web app might be a placeholder, he says, or the app might be just a proof of concept.

He compares the ongoing deluge of data exposures that are resulting from companies' unsecured AI-coded web apps to the epidemic of exposed data created by the security settings of Amazon S3 storage buckets in earlier years.

extraction.body: Security researcher Dor Zvi and his team at the cybersecurity firm he cofounded, RedAccess, analyzed thousands of vibe-coded web applications created using the AI software development tools Lovable, Replit, Base44, and Netlify and found more than 5,000 of them that had virtually no security or authentication of any kind. Many of these web apps allowed anyone who merely finds their web URL to access the apps and their data. Around 40 percent of the apps exposed sensitive data, Zvi says, including medical information, financial data, corporate presentations, and strategy documents, as well as detailed logs of customer conversations with chatbots. “The end result is that organizations are actually leaking private data through vibe-coding applications,” says Zvi. “This is one of the biggest events ever where people are exposing corporate or other sensitive information to anyone in the world.” Zvi says RedAccess’ scouring for vulnerable web apps was surprisingly easy. Lovable, Replit, Base44, and Netlify all allow users to host their web apps on those AI companies' own domains, rather than the users’. So the researchers used straightforward Google and Bing searches for those AI companies' domains combined with other search terms to identify thousands of apps that had been vibe coded with the companies' tools. Of the 5,000 AI-coded apps that Zvi says were left publicly accessible to anyone who simply typed their URLs into a browser, he found close to 2,000 that, upon closer inspection, seemed to reveal private data: Screenshots of web apps he shared with WIRED—several of which WIRED verified were still online and exposed—showed what appeared to be a hospital's work assignments with the personally identifiable information of doctors, a company's detailed ad purchasing information, what appeared to be another firm's go-to-market strategy presentation, a retailer's full logs of its chatbot's conversations with customers, including the customers' full names and contact information, a shipping firm's cargo records, and assorted sales and financial records from a variety of other companies. In some cases, Zvi says, he found that the exposed apps would have allowed him to gain administrative privileges over systems and even remove other administrators. In the case of Lovable, Zvi says he also found numerous examples of phishing sites that impersonated major corporations, including Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe’s, and McDonald’s, that appeared to have been created with the AI coding tool and hosted on Lovable's domain. When WIRED asked the four AI coding companies about RedAccess’ findings, Netlify didn’t respond, but the three other companies pushed back on the researchers’ claims and protested that they hadn't shared enough of their findings or provided enough time for them to respond. (RedAccess says it reached out to the companies on Monday.) But they didn't deny that the web apps RedAccess found were left exposed. “From the limited information they shared, [RedAccess's] core claim appears to be that some users have published apps on the open web that should’ve been private,” Replit's CEO Amjad Masad wrote in a response post on X. “Replit allows users to choose whether apps are public or private. Public apps being accessible on the internet is expected behavior. Privacy settings can be changed at any time with a single click.” A spokesperson for Lovable responded in a statement that “Lovable takes reports of exposed data and phishing sites seriously, and we're actively working to obtain what we need to investigate. It's also worth noting that Lovable gives builders the tools to build securely, but how an app is configured is ultimately the creator's responsibility.” Blake Brodie, the head of public relations for Base44's parent company, Wix, wrote in a statement that “Base44 provides users with robust tools to configure their own applications' security, including access controls and visibility settings.” She added that “disabling those controls is a deliberate, straightforward action, any user can do it. Where applications were publicly accessible, that reflects a user configuration choice, not a platform vulnerability.” Brodie also noted that “it is trivially easy to fabricate applications that appear to contain real user data. Without a single verified example provided to us, we have no way to assess the validity of these claims.” RedAccess, for its part, disputed that it hadn't provided examples to Base44. Zvi notes that for a few dozen exposed web apps, it went so far as to contact the app's apparent owner, which confirmed that data had been exposed. RedAccess also shared with WIRED anonymized communications in several cases that showed Base44 users thanking the researchers for alerting them to exposed web apps, which were then secured or taken offline. Verifying whether real data has been exposed on any particular unsecured AI-coded web app can be tricky, says Joel Margolis, a security researcher who, along with a colleague, recently discovered that an AI chat toy had exposed 50,000 conversations the toy had with children on a website with virtually no security. Data in a vibe-coded web app might be a placeholder, he says, or the app might be just a proof of concept. Wix’s Brodie argued that two examples that WIRED shared with Base44 did appear to be test sites or have AI-generated data. For the web apps WIRED reviewed, we couldn't confirm that the personal or corporate data was as sensitive—or real—as it appeared to be. Margolis nonetheless says that the problem of AI-built web apps exposing data is very real. “Somebody from a marketing team wants to create a website. And unless you ask them to do it securely, they're not going to go out of their way to do that.” Zvi points out that the 5,000 exposed apps Red Access found were only those hosted on the AI coding tools' own domains, and that likely thousands more are hosted on users' own purchased domains. He compares the ongoing deluge of data exposures that are resulting from companies' unsecured AI-coded web apps to the epidemic of exposed data created by the security settings of Amazon S3 storage buckets in earlier years. Companies from Verizon to World Wrestling Entertainment accidentally exposed reams of sensitive data due to misconfigurations in their instance of Amazon's cloud storage service. AI web-app coding tools are now creating a wave of data exposures, the result of a similar combination of user error and lack of safeguards, Zvi says. Yet more fundamental than any particular security failing on the part of the AI coding companies, he argues, is simply that these tools allow a new class of people within organizations to create applications—often with little security awareness and outside the usual software development processes that companies use to vet applications before they're released. “Anyone from your company at any moment can generate an app, and this is not going through any development cycle or any security check,” Zvi says. “People can just start using it in production without asking anyone.

sources.title: I Vibe Coded the One Mac Feature Apple Won't Build—and Put It on the App Store for You
passages: I found an app called Hotkeys that seemed to do what I wanted, but it left the App Store quite a while ago, presumably because it was designed for Intel-based hardware. (Apple is ending support for such apps with macOS 28.) You May Also Like But now that Golden Gate has deeper Apple Intelligence tools, I decided to use Claude Code and Xcode to vibe code a modern, intuitive, and unobtrusive hotkey app called KeyRun.
You can tell Claude not to waste tokens by complimenting you, but even an AI agent’s praise is good to have, so I didn't.
I also had Claude build a “save” feature that saves a set of keyboard shortcuts to a file, so that I could copy the file to another system and use the same hotkeys.

extraction.body: I've always wanted a straightforward way to launch apps, open documents in their default apps, or bring up folders on macOS via hotkeys. To do the same in macOS, you either have to build a multistep process via the Shortcuts app or download a third-party utility such as FastScripts 3 , HomeRow , Karabiner-Elements , Keyboard Maestro , or Raycast . These apps and others that I've tried work, but they are either unnecessarily complex or cost more than I want to spend. I found an app called Hotkeys that seemed to do what I wanted, but it left the App Store quite a while ago, presumably because it was designed for Intel-based hardware. (Apple is ending support for such apps with macOS 28.) You May Also Like But now that Golden Gate has deeper Apple Intelligence tools, I decided to use Claude Code and Xcode to vibe code a modern, intuitive, and unobtrusive hotkey app called KeyRun. And, of course, I made it free for anyone to download from the Mac App Store. Setting Up the AI Workbench in macOS Golden Gate Apple’s Xcode programming app already had AI integrations in macOS Sequoia , but the connections are tighter in the Golden Gate beta. For one, your conversations now take place in the main Xcode window rather than in a sidebar. Installing Claude (Credit: Apple/PCMag) To get started, you’ll need a Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini chatbot account. Then, in Xcode, simply go to Settings > Intelligence and click Get next to the agent you want to install. I chose Claude and got right into prompting . Prompting KeyRun to Life—and Bypassing Mac's Permissions Trap I began by asking Claude, “Can you create a simple, intuitive macOS app that assigns hotkeys to applications, so that I can submit it to the App Store? I want the app to create a hotkey for any app that I either drag into the app’s window or choose from a list of files.” Claude complied, and in a few seconds, it coded an app that matched my specifications. I was able to view the actual code by opening its files from the Xcode sidebar. I then asked Claude to rewrite the app so that it wouldn’t create hotkeys that macOS already uses , such as Cmd-Q (quit the current app) or Cmd-S (save the current document). It agreed to this and subsequently made the app check any new shortcuts against the list of system-wide hotkeys that macOS maintains in the background. Coding with Claude (Credit: Apple/PCMag) But then I hit a complication. When I tried to use a hotkey I had created, macOS told me I needed to grant it Accessibility permission in the System Settings app. I didn’t want prospective users to deal with this annoyance, so I asked Claude if a workaround was possible. Claude immediately solved the problem by rewriting the app’s hotkey mechanism to use Apple’s ancient Carbon framework instead of the modern AppKit’s global event monitor. Apple officially states that Carbon, in general, is deprecated, but it never explicitly got rid of the Carbon hotkey mechanism and has even updated it for 64-bit macOS environments. Almost all existing hotkey apps use this mechanism, so it's not likely to go away anytime soon. At this point, Claude suggested that we save the project and give it a name. Claude, sounding like a restaurant waiter who says “Excellent Choice!” no matter what you choose from the menu, told me it was an excellent name. You can tell Claude not to waste tokens by complimenting you, but even an AI agent’s praise is good to have, so I didn't. Then, I got ambitious and asked Claude to add a feature that could open documents, not only apps, from a hotkey. Claude did exactly that, adding the detail that it would add only those documents that normally open in a default app when you double-click on them. I pushed things further by asking for an option to open folders with hotkeys. Every time Claude added a feature, I thought of another. I also had Claude build a “save” feature that saves a set of keyboard shortcuts to a file, so that I could copy the file to another system and use the same hotkeys. After that, I had Claude add profiles so I could use a different set of hotkeys when working on documents and editing images. Finally, I asked Claude to create a hotkey for KeyRun itself. KeyRun app interface (Credit: Ed Mendelson/PCMag) At every stage, Claude and I consulted on which keyboard shortcuts to use in the app’s menus for each new feature. Claude suggested that the app should automatically delete the hotkey assignment if it couldn’t find the app or document associated with it, but I reminded Claude that the user might decide to bring back the app or document, and that the user should be able to decide whether to keep or delete an obsolete hotkey assignment—and Claude agreed. The last thing I did was add an option to launch KeyRun automatically upon startup. Surviving the App Store Review: Beta Bugs and Rejections When the app seemed complete, I asked Claude to guide me through submitting it to the Mac App Store. Of course, if you want to create an app just for personal needs, you can skip these steps.

extraction.body: An OpenAI employee was arrested after a " sophisticated recording device " was discovered inside its executive conference room, according to the Department of Justice and a post by the company. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who is a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9 in connection with the matter, the DOJ said in a release on Tuesday. The company said an employee planted the device a few days before it was found, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation "moved quickly to make an arrest," the post said. The employee was terminated. FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology." "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI said in the post. "We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance." Alfozan was not authorized to access the executive conference room where the device was found, according to the DOJ. The department said footage showed him near the conference room on multiple days before the device was discovered. The DOJ said that on Oct. 5, he went into the room. The DOJ said a bag was also found in the OpenAI building on or about Oct. 5 that belonged to Alfozan. Inside the bag, security found his wallet, ID and another recording device similar to the one that was in the executive conference room. The department said a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse that "shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan's own chatbot account" was used to get information about continuous audio recording and Wi-Fi. The DOJ said promps were submitted related to "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device." The device was concealed in toilet paper, and its contents were encrypted, according to the DOJ. This security incident comes as the ChatGPT-maker, along with competitors like Anthropic and other big tech names, faces heightened scrutiny over safety protocols after a series of cyber incidents where autonomous agents escaped testing environments and hacked into outside systems. Last week, OpenAI defended its decision to fire three safety researchers, alleging a "significant breach of trust," saying that the researchers "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information." Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni raised safety concerns in a letter to OpenAI's leadership, saying that communications around their exits "have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI." The employee was identified as Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national. Alfozan is charged with using or endeavoring to use a device to intercept oral communications, according to a press release from the Department of Justice. Alfozan didn’t have access to this room, but CCTV footage allegedly showed him “near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery,” according to the DOJ. Additionally, the DOJ claims OpenAI security discovered a bag Alfozan left in another room inside the company’s office, where they found his wallet, ID, and another recording device. OpenAI says it fired the employee and referred the incident to the FBI. Alfozan was arrested Friday and has remained in custody since, appearing in federal court for the first time on Tuesday. > We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. extraction.body: OpenAI said it has alerted the FBI after discovering that an employee allegedly planted a hidden recording device in one of the AI maker’s office executive conference rooms. The employee, named by federal prosecutors as Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, was fired and arrested on October 9, about a week after OpenAI discovered the surveillance device. The company said in a post on X that it used its internal AI models to understand the “sophisticated” device. OpenAI told TechCrunch that the device contained “advanced encryption, audio monitoring capabilities, and a mechanism for transferring data designed to evade monitoring,” though it is unclear to what degree this device is technically distinct from other recording devices. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” said OpenAI in its post on X. OpenAI’s spokesperson, Nate Evans, confirmed that the employee started with the AI model maker in July 2025 and worked on the product team. Prosecutors with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of California said Alfozan was charged with using an electronic device to intercept oral communications — effectively accusing him of covertly recording people’s voice audio without their permission. Prosecutors said OpenAI caught the device after it was inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in OpenAI’s San Francisco office. Per the prosecutors, Alfozan was caught looking behind the television where the recording device was placed, and where OpenAI had placed a camera that allegedly caught the employee. It’s not clear exactly for what purpose the recording device was used, but FBI director Kash Patel said the scheme was to “capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology.” Neither Alfozan nor his attorney could be immediately reached for comment. He faces five years in prison if convicted. When reached, a spokesperson for the FBI reiterated a statement made by Patel. “Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” Patel said.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who is a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9 in connection with the matter, the DOJ said in a release on Tuesday. The company said an employee planted the device a few days before it was found, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation "moved quickly to make an arrest," the post said. The employee was terminated. FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology." "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI said in the post. "We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance." Alfozan was not authorized to access the executive conference room where the device was found, according to the DOJ. The department said footage showed him near the conference room on multiple days before the device was discovered. The DOJ said that on Oct. 5, he went into the room. The DOJ said a bag was also found in the OpenAI building on or about Oct. 5 that belonged to Alfozan. Inside the bag, security found his wallet, ID and another recording device similar to the one that was in the executive conference room. The department said a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse that "shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan's own chatbot account" was used to get information about continuous audio recording and Wi-Fi. The DOJ said promps were submitted related to "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device." The device was concealed in toilet paper, and its contents were encrypted, according to the DOJ. This security incident comes as the ChatGPT-maker, along with competitors like Anthropic and other big tech names, faces heightened scrutiny over safety protocols after a series of cyber incidents where autonomous agents escaped testing environments and hacked into outside systems. Last week, OpenAI defended its decision to fire three safety researchers, alleging a "significant breach of trust," saying that the researchers "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information." Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni raised safety concerns in a letter to OpenAI's leadership, saying that communications around their exits "have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI." When reached, a spokesperson for the FBI reiterated a statement made by Patel. “Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” Patel said.

The new products are co-developed by LG Electronics and Apple, and work seamlessly with Apple devices. NEW YORK, Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LG Electronics (LG) today announced a range of smart home accessories co-developed with Apple for the Apple Home Collection, including indoor and outdoor cameras, and a video doorbell, smart lock, smart thermostat and temperature sensor. The new products are designed to make the everyday home experience simpler, more reliable and seamlessly connected and private in Apple Home. These smart home accessories represent LG's commitment to creating connected and adaptive experiences. They also advance the company's ambition to simplify everyday living by reducing the need for manual intervention and enabling more intuitive interactions between customers and their environments. "Creating a truly connected home requires products that work seamlessly together," said Kihyun Jung, head of the Platform Business Center at the LG Home Appliance Solution Company. "By bringing LG's expertise in home appliances and the home environment together with the Apple Home, we are creating intuitive, integrated experiences that fit naturally into customers' daily lives." "Apple has always focused on making products and experiences that are seamless and intuitive, and protect our users' privacy — and that matters more than ever in the home," said Matthew Costello, Apple's vice president of Hardware Engineering. "Combining our hardware and software expertise with LG's deep understanding of the home and connected living lets us build smart home experiences that are simpler to set up, are easier to control, and work effortlessly." Moving Beyond Connectivity to Co-Develop Products and User Experiences Moving beyond just device compatibility, Apple and LG developed these new products together from the early product planning stage, collaborating on hardware, software and user experiences. Each product is designed with a consistent user experience in mind to streamline setup and control. Rather than simply linking individual products through a platform, the accessories are designed to work together. Using the Home app or Siri to control a single "Good Morning" scene can simultaneously adjust the thermostat and tilt an indoor camera down while a user is getting ready.1 And each accessory is encrypted end-to-end in Apple Home, so only users and the people they choose can access their home data. Introducing New Indoor and Outdoor Cameras, a Video Doorbell, Smart Lock, Thermostat and Temperature Sensor Starting in December, with select accessories coming early next year, LG and Apple are launching the full lineup in the United States and Canada, including indoor and outdoor cameras, a video doorbell, a smart lock, a thermostat and a temperature sensor with support for Apple Home and LG ThinQ apps.1 In the United Kingdom, indoor and outdoor cameras and a video doorbell will be available starting December.2 Cameras LG's new indoor and outdoor cameras deliver clear imaging, intelligent detection and privacy-focused controls to help users monitor what matters around their homes. With up to 2.5K video resolution, low-light color night vision, and wide-angle coverage, the cameras provide clear views during the day and at night. Using intelligence, each camera recognizes people, pets, vehicles and motion, helping deliver more relevant alerts and reducing unnecessary notifications. Users can also block selected areas from view and recording, while built-in local storage provides greater control over how recorded footage is stored and reviewed. LG Indoor Cam Plug-In : A wide 160° field of view captures more of the room in a single frame, while a privacy tilt mechanism and physical controls provide a visible and intuitive way to control monitoring when it is not needed. LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In : The camera provides reliable outdoor monitoring with low light color night vision, and 2.5K resolution, helping users maintain a clear view around the home day and night. LG Floodlight Cam : The camera adds dual adaptive floodlights that automatically illuminate the surrounding area when activity is detected, combining outdoor monitoring and lighting in one integrated home security solution. LG Video Doorbell Wired LG Video Doorbell Wired brings clear visibility, more relevant alerts and everyday convenience to the front door. Its dual-camera system combines a 2.5K front camera and a Full HD bottom camera, capturing separate views of visitors, packages and key areas around the entryway for broader coverage. It can also identify people, vehicles, pets and packages and play a helpful chime through Apple HomeView, HomePod or HomePod mini. Low-light color night vision and two-way talk also help users see and respond to activity at their door. LG Smart Deadbolt Lock LG Smart Deadbolt Lock combines smart access, minimal design and everyday convenience, led by hands-free unlocking with home key on a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch and advanced Ultra-Wideband technology. The lock recognizes an authorized user's location and movement to support reliable hands-free entry. NFC tap, PIN code and a physical key provide additional ways to unlock the door, while built-in door sensing and real-time app notifications help users monitor door status and security events. LG Smart Thermostat and LG Temperature Sensor LG Smart Thermostat combines energy efficiency, intuitive design to make home comfort more adaptive and efficient. Adaptive Temperature from Apple can adjust heating and cooling based on headed home, away from home or sleeping. When paired with optional LG Temperature Sensor devices placed in other rooms, the system can monitor temperature and humidity across multiple spaces to support more consistent comfort throughout the home. Advanced sensing algorithms are designed to reduce measurement errors and detect indoor temperature changes in real time, while Matter over Thread enables low-power, responsive connectivity with fewer connection delays and offline disruptions. In the U.S., Clean Energy Guidance from Apple can help optimize energy use based on grid carbon intensity. Through supported utility-provider integrations, LG Smart Thermostat can also shift operation toward lower-cost periods. Privacy in Apple Home Privacy is foundational to Apple Home. Camera footage and personal data in the Home app is stored end-to-end encrypted and never accessible to LG or Apple. 1 Use of the new IoT products requires an Apple home hub, like HomePod, HomePod mini, Apple TV 4K or Apple HomeView. The new IoT products, the LG ThinQ, and the Apple Home require a Wi-Fi connection. Available services, features and compatibility may vary depending on product model, region and country. 2 Product availability, including availability at retail stores, may vary by region and country. LG's four Companies – Home Appliance Solution, Media Entertainment Solution, Vehicle Solution and the Eco Solution – combined for global revenue of over KRW 89 trillion in 2025. LG is a leading manufacturer of consumer and commercial products ranging from TVs, home appliances, air solutions, monitors, automotive components and solutions, and its premium LG SIGNATURE and intelligent LG ThinQ brands are familiar names the world over. Visit www.lg.com/global/newsroom for the latest news.

Apple worked closely with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric to create an integrated Apple Home experience across the new product lineup. And like all accessories in Apple Home, Apple Home Collection products are designed for privacy, with Home app data encrypted end-to-end, so LG Electronics, Schneider Electric, and Apple can’t read it. These new Apple Home Collection products feature a clean, minimal aesthetic and premium materials, with every detail considered, from how they mount and adjust to how they look and feel alongside Apple products throughout the home. Each product can be set up starting with a single tap with iPhone, controlled entirely from the Home app and using Siri, and work as either standalone accessories or together as a connected system. “LG Electronics has spent decades developing technologies and products designed around the way people live,” said Kihyun Jung, LG Electronics’ executive vice president. “Working closely with Apple, we’ve co-created a more connected, intuitive, and convenient home experience for our customers.” “As a global leader in energy technology, we are proud to bring our experience in innovative and advanced climate control to Apple Home,” said Olivier Blum, Schneider Electric’s CEO. “Schneider Home’s new Smart Thermostat is a true collaboration with Apple to give customers a seamless way to help manage their home’s energy use, effortlessly blending efficiency with everyday comfort and simplicity.” LG’s lineup of four cameras gives users a private and intelligent way to monitor their homes when using a home hub like Apple HomeView, HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K. Every camera captures up to 2.5K resolution video and recognizes people, familiar faces, pets, vehicles, and packages, with video history securely stored in users’ supported iCloud+ plan, so there’s no separate camera subscription. 2 Each camera works with iCloud+, giving users access to 10 days’ worth of event video history. On eligible iCloud+ plans, Apple Intelligence adds automatic video descriptions that summarize what’s happening in a clip, along with the ability to search footage using natural, descriptive language. 3 Built-in storage keeps cameras recording even when Wi-Fi goes down, and improvements to the way footage is captured and stored ensure detected moments aren’t missed during a network outage. Users can view live footage and camera activity at any time right from the Home app on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple TV 4K, or HomeView — with quick live snapshots that give an at-a-glance view without needing to open a full livestream. LG’s Smart Deadbolt Lock brings a new level of convenience to home access. Using Ultra Wideband technology, the lock can tell how close a user is and when they’re approaching the door. As a user with a home key on a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch walks up, the door unlocks automatically, with no tapping required. For flexibility, users can also tap to unlock with an iPhone or Apple Watch, use an integrated PIN pad, or rely on a hidden backup key slot. The lock can sense if the door has been opened, closed, or tampered with, alerting users if it’s open even while locked. Guest access can also be shared directly through the Home app, making it simple to grant a dog walker, house sitter, or visiting family member their own way in. Controls in the Home app allow the doorbell and lock to work together as a front-door system — letting users see who’s there and unlock the door in a single view or by asking Siri. When a visitor rings the bell, a chime sounds through HomeView, HomePod, or HomePod mini, and a notification appears on the user’s Apple devices, like iPhone or iPad. From wherever they are, users can see who’s at the door, speak to the visitor, and unlock the door for them. The new smart lock is Matter compatible and supports Aliro, working entirely locally so core access functions continue even without an internet connection. Two new Smart Thermostats are available — one from LG Electronics and one from Schneider Electric — so users can choose the product that best fits their home’s broader energy ecosystem. Using on-device intelligence from iPhone, Adaptive Temperature in the Home app automatically adjusts the thermostats based on whether someone is at home, winding down at night, or away, ensuring the home is always at the right temperature without any manual scheduling. In the contiguous U.S., Clean Energy Guidance can shift heating and cooling to cleaner, lower-cost periods for users with a compatible utility plan, and the Home app displays usage insights over time, including peak and off-peak rate information. The new thermostats can read temperature and humidity across multiple rooms using LG Electronics’ and Schneider Electric’s new standalone temperature and humidity sensors, or the sensors already built into HomeView, HomePod, and HomePod mini. Both thermostats and temperature and humidity sensors are Matter compatible and DIY-friendly, and work with a broad range of HVAC systems, with on-device wire detection to simplify installation. Every product across the new lineup shares a consistent, seamless setup and control experience. Starting with a single tap with iPhone, the accessory is added to Apple Home, similar to setting up HomePod — with no additional app to download and no separate account to create. Every device supports Thread, helping it maintain connectivity even if a Wi-Fi connection drops. Products also automatically update their network credentials if a customer changes their home Wi-Fi, eliminating a common smart home frustration. The accessories are designed to work together, and users can control every product with Siri. A single “Good Morning” scene can simultaneously adjust the thermostat, tilt an indoor camera down while a user is getting ready, and start music on HomePod. Using on-device intelligence from iPhone or Apple Watch, users can set up Apple Home to recognize key moments throughout the day: As the last user leaves for work, the thermostat adjusts for an empty home, the door locks, and cameras begin monitoring again. Before they arrive home, the thermostat begins adjusting the temperature, and the front door unlocks automatically as they approach. Privacy is foundational to Apple Home. Camera footage and personal data in the Home app are stored end-to-end encrypted and never accessible to LG Electronics, Schneider Electric, or Apple. Camera footage is securely processed locally on the customer’s own Apple Home hub or in Private Cloud Compute and, for users with iCloud+, stored encrypted in iCloud for 10 days. No one, not even Apple, can access the data. Professional Installation Available at Apple Retail For customers who prefer to have their smart home accessories professionally installed, Apple Retail now offers third-party installation from ADT for an additional charge, available in the U.S. starting this fall. Apple revolutionized personal technology with the introduction of the Macintosh in 1984. Today, Apple leads the world in innovation with iPhone, iPad, Mac, AirPods, Apple Watch, and Apple Vision Pro. Apple’s six software platforms — iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, visionOS, and tvOS — provide seamless experiences across all Apple devices and empower people with breakthrough services including the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Pay, iCloud, and Apple TV. As a user with a home key on a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch® walks up, the door unlocks automatically, with no tapping required. For flexibility, users can also tap to unlock with an iPhone or Apple Watch, use an integrated PIN pad, or rely on a hidden backup key slot. The lock can sense if the door has been opened, closed, or tampered with, alerting users if it’s open even while locked. Guest access can also be shared directly through the Home app, making it simple to grant a dog walker, house sitter, or visiting family member their own way in.

Controls in the Home app allow the doorbell and lock to work together as a front-door system — letting users see who’s there and unlock the door in a single view or by asking Siri®. When a visitor rings the bell, a chime sounds through HomeView, HomePod, or HomePod mini, and a notification appears on the user’s Apple devices, like iPhone or iPad. From wherever they are, users can see who’s at the door, speak to the visitor, and unlock the door for them. The new smart lock is Matter compatible and supports Aliro, working entirely locally so core access functions continue even without an internet connection.

Two new Smart Thermostats are available — one from LG Electronics and one from Schneider Electric — so users can choose the product that best fits their home’s broader energy ecosystem. Using on-device intelligence from iPhone, Adaptive Temperature in the Home app automatically adjusts the thermostats based on whether someone is at home, winding down at night, or away, ensuring the home is always at the right temperature without any manual scheduling.

In the contiguous U.S., Clean Energy Guidance can shift heating and cooling to cleaner, lower-cost periods for users with a compatible utility plan, and the Home app displays usage insights over time, including peak and off-peak rate information. The new thermostats can read temperature and humidity across multiple rooms using LG Electronics’ and Schneider Electric’s new standalone temperature and humidity sensors, or the sensors already built into HomeView, HomePod, and HomePod mini.
Both thermostats and temperature and humidity sensors are Matter compatible and DIY-friendly, and work with a broad range of HVAC systems, with on-device wire detection to simplify installation.

Every product across the new lineup shares a consistent, seamless setup and control experience. Starting with a single tap with iPhone, the accessory is added to Apple Home, similar to setting up HomePod — with no additional app to download and no separate account to create. Every device supports Thread, helping it maintain connectivity even if a Wi-Fi connection drops. Products also automatically update their network credentials if a customer changes their home Wi-Fi, eliminating a common smart home frustration.

The accessories are designed to work together, and users can control every product with Siri. A single “Good Morning” scene can simultaneously adjust the thermostat, tilt an indoor camera down while a user is getting ready, and start music on HomePod. Using on-device intelligence from iPhone or Apple Watch, users can set up Apple Home to recognize key moments throughout the day: As the last user leaves for work, the thermostat adjusts for an empty home, the door locks, and cameras begin monitoring again. Before they arrive home, the thermostat begins adjusting the temperature, and the front door unlocks automatically as they approach.

Privacy is foundational to Apple Home. Camera footage and personal data in the Home app are stored end-to-end encrypted and never accessible to LG Electronics, Schneider Electric, or Apple. Camera footage is securely processed locally on the customer’s own Apple Home hub or in Private Cloud Compute and, for users with iCloud+, stored encrypted in iCloud® for 10 days. No one, not even Apple, can access the data.
Professional Installation Available at Apple Retail

For customers who prefer to have their smart home accessories professionally installed, Apple Retail now offers third-party installation from ADT for an additional charge, available in the U.S. starting this fall.

Apple’s six software platforms — iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, visionOS, and tvOS — provide seamless experiences across all Apple devices and empower people with breakthrough services including the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Pay, iCloud, and Apple TV. Apple’s more than 150,000 employees are dedicated to making the best products on earth and to leaving the world better than we found it.

Apple worked closely with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric to create an integrated Apple Home experience across the new product lineup. And like all accessories in Apple Home, Apple Home Collection products are designed for privacy, with Home app data encrypted end-to-end, so LG Electronics, Schneider Electric, and Apple can’t read it.

These new Apple Home Collection products feature a clean, minimal aesthetic and premium materials, with every detail considered, from how they mount and adjust to how they look and feel alongside Apple products throughout the home. Each product can be set up starting with a single tap with iPhone, controlled entirely from the Home app and using Siri, and work as either standalone accessories or together as a connected system.

“LG Electronics has spent decades developing technologies and products designed around the way people live,” said Kihyun Jung, LG Electronics’ executive vice president. “Working closely with Apple, we’ve co-created a more connected, intuitive, and convenient home experience for our customers.”

“As a global leader in energy technology, we are proud to bring our experience in innovative and advanced climate control to Apple Home,” said Olivier Blum, Schneider Electric’s CEO. “Schneider Home’s new Smart Thermostat is a true collaboration with Apple to give customers a seamless way to help manage their home’s energy use, effortlessly blending efficiency with everyday comfort and simplicity.”

LG’s lineup of four cameras gives users a private and intelligent way to monitor their homes when using a home hub like Apple HomeView, HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K. Every camera captures up to 2.5K resolution video and recognizes people, familiar faces, pets, vehicles, and packages, with video history securely stored in users’ supported iCloud+ plan, so there’s no separate camera subscription. 2

Each camera works with iCloud+, giving users access to 10 days’ worth of event video history. On eligible iCloud+ plans, Apple Intelligence adds automatic video descriptions that summarize what’s happening in a clip, along with the ability to search footage using natural, descriptive language. 3 Built-in storage keeps cameras recording even when Wi-Fi goes down, and improvements to the way footage is captured and stored ensure detected moments aren’t missed during a network outage. Users can view live footage and camera activity at any time right from the Home app on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple TV 4K, or HomeView — with quick live snapshots that give an at-a-glance view without needing to open a full livestream.

LG’s Smart Deadbolt Lock brings a new level of convenience to home access. Using Ultra Wideband technology, the lock can tell how close a user is and when they’re approaching the door. As a user with a home key on a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch walks up, the door unlocks automatically, with no tapping required. For flexibility, users can also tap to unlock with an iPhone or Apple Watch, use an integrated PIN pad, or rely on a hidden backup key slot. The lock can sense if the door has been opened, closed, or tampered with, alerting users if it’s open even while locked. Guest access can also be shared directly through the Home app, making it simple to grant a dog walker, house sitter, or visiting family member their own way in.

Controls in the Home app allow the doorbell and lock to work together as a front-door system — letting users see who’s there and unlock the door in a single view or by asking Siri. When a visitor rings the bell, a chime sounds through HomeView, HomePod, or HomePod mini, and a notification appears on the user’s Apple devices, like iPhone or iPad. From wherever they are, users can see who’s at the door, speak to the visitor, and unlock the door for them. The new smart lock is Matter compatible and supports Aliro, working entirely locally so core access functions continue even without an internet connection.

Two new Smart Thermostats are available — one from LG Electronics and one from Schneider Electric — so users can choose the product that best fits their home’s broader energy ecosystem. Using on-device intelligence from iPhone, Adaptive Temperature in the Home app automatically adjusts the thermostats based on whether someone is at home, winding down at night, or away, ensuring the home is always at the right temperature without any manual scheduling.

In the contiguous U.S., Clean Energy Guidance can shift heating and cooling to cleaner, lower-cost periods for users with a compatible utility plan, and the Home app displays usage insights over time, including peak and off-peak rate information. The new thermostats can read temperature and humidity across multiple rooms using LG Electronics’ and Schneider Electric’s new standalone temperature and humidity sensors, or the sensors already built into HomeView, HomePod, and HomePod mini.
Both thermostats and temperature and humidity sensors are Matter compatible and DIY-friendly, and work with a broad range of HVAC systems, with on-device wire detection to simplify installation.

Every product across the new lineup shares a consistent, seamless setup and control experience. Starting with a single tap with iPhone, the accessory is added to Apple Home, similar to setting up HomePod — with no additional app to download and no separate account to create. Every device supports Thread, helping it maintain connectivity even if a Wi-Fi connection drops. Products also automatically update their network credentials if a customer changes their home Wi-Fi, eliminating a common smart home frustration.

The accessories are designed to work together, and users can control every product with Siri. A single “Good Morning” scene can simultaneously adjust the thermostat, tilt an indoor camera down while a user is getting ready, and start music on HomePod. Using on-device intelligence from iPhone or Apple Watch, users can set up Apple Home to recognize key moments throughout the day: As the last user leaves for work, the thermostat adjusts for an empty home, the door locks, and cameras begin monitoring again. Before they arrive home, the thermostat begins adjusting the temperature, and the front door unlocks automatically as they approach.

Privacy is foundational to Apple Home. Camera footage and personal data in the Home app are stored end-to-end encrypted and never accessible to LG Electronics, Schneider Electric, or Apple. Camera footage is securely processed locally on the customer’s own Apple Home hub or in Private Cloud Compute and, for users with iCloud+, stored encrypted in iCloud for 10 days. No one, not even Apple, can access the data.

For customers who prefer to have their smart home accessories professionally installed, Apple Retail now offers third-party installation from ADT for an additional charge, available in the U.S. starting this fall.

sources.title: Apple sues OpenAI, its employees claiming theft of trade secrets - BBC
passages: Apple said in its lawsuit that, because OpenAI's "misconduct is normalized and exemplified by leadership" its "nascent hardware business now rests on the shakiest of foundations, rotten to its core by its illegal reliance on misappropriated trade secrets".

In a federal lawsuit filed on Friday, Apple sued the artificial intelligence (AI) company, two of its employees, as well as io Products, claiming it has engaged in "a pattern of theft" of Apple's confidential product development and related work.
Drew Pusateri, a spokesman for OpenAI, told the BBC: "We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets."

Through these former employees and their access to "sensitive projects, trusted partner relationships, proprietary manufacturing techniques, and unreleased products," Apple claims OpenAI has been able to glean details of its product plans and operations.
Apple added that when OpenAI interviews current Apple employees for potential jobs the company allegedly tries to extract further information from them.

It is also suing Chang Liu, a senior electrical engineer who worked at Apple for eight years, and Tang Yew Tan, a vice president of design for iPhone and Apple Watch who spent 24 years with the company.
At least two long-time Apple workers who left the company to join OpenAI allegedly took part in this pattern by, in part, emailing themselves internal Apple information.
OpenAI interviewers allegedly have told the prospective hires to "bring 'actual parts' as 'props' from Apple for 'show and tell'" during their interview.
Apple has asked the court to immediately prohibit OpenAI from obtaining or using any alleged confidential information and it is seeking unspecified monetary damages.
It represents a major shift in relations between Apple and OpenAI, creator of the popular AI chatbot ChatGPT.
Yet, when Cook revealed in April that he was stepping down, Sam Altman, co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, publicly praised him as "a legend", adding he was "very thankful for everything he has done".
Tim Cook, Apple's outgoing CEO, had added ChatGPT into Apple devices as the company was looking to offer more AI features.
This year, Apple shifted more of its AI features to run on Google's Gemini model and tools.
OpenAI is expected to release its first hardware product, a type of keyboard to be used with its AI tools, this month.
The company also said that it had attempted to discuss it's concerns with OpenAI in February, but was ultimately ignored.

sources.title: Apple sues OpenAI, alleging artificial intelligence company stole trade secrets - The Guardian
passages: Apple filed a lawsuit against OpenAI on Friday alleging the artificial intelligence firm stole company trade secrets in a move to create its own hardware device.
“OpenAI’s nascent hardware business now rests on the shakiest of foundations, rotten to its core by its illegal reliance on misappropriated trade secrets,” Apple wrote in its complaint.
Tang Yew Tan, OpenAI’s chief hardware officer and a former vice-president at Apple, is named in the suit.
Apple alleges that Tan took information about Apple suppliers with him to OpenAI and encouraged interviewees at OpenAI to divulge confidential company information.

“Recently, significant evidence has emerged suggesting individuals employed by OpenAI wrongfully took Apple’s secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes and products,” an Apple spokesperson said in an email.
Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company was reviewing the court filing.
“We have no interest in other companies’ trade secrets,” he added.
“We remain focused on building innovative technology that empowers people everywhere.”
Apple’s lawsuit is a sharp turnaround for the two tech giants, which announced a major partnership in 2024.
That deal involved Apple integrating OpenAI’s chatbot, ChatGPT, into the operating systems for iPhones, iPads and Macs.
But when Apple showcased its revamped voice assistant Siri last month, its AI component was based on Google’s Gemini AI model, rather than ChatGPT.

Tensions between the two companies began to simmer last year when OpenAI spent $6.4bn to acquire a hardware startup founded by former Apple design guru Jony Ive, indicating that the AI titan was foraying into hardware.
The company is seeking damages and a court order that would block OpenAI from possessing or using its trade secrets.
The suit claims OpenAI poached Apple employees, coaxing them to hand over confidential material, product designs and other tightly held information.

“He has directed job candidates still working for Apple to bring ‘actual parts’ from Apple to their interviews for ‘show and tell’ sessions in which he and his team at OpenAI can elicit still more Apple confidential information,” reads Apple’s complaint.

passages: A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI’s hiring materials in the trade secrets-focused lawsuit the iPhone maker filed against OpenAI in July.

The court gave OpenAI five days to turn over materials it has already collected and 14 days for any other materials related to this request, agreeing with Apple that these documents should be expedited.

In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data.
Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations.

The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone — or smartphones more generally — if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers’ lives and how they engage with software and services.
That denial isn’t final, though; the judge left the door open for Apple to narrow its requests and try again.

These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components.

In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data. Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations. The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone — or smartphones more generally — if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers’ lives and how they engage with software and services. That denial isn’t final, though; the judge left the door open for Apple to narrow its requests and try again. These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components.
