Specifically, the court will allow Apple to view documents associated with OpenAI’s interviews with former Apple employees who applied for roles within its consumer hardware and robotics groups ahead of the rumored launch of OpenAI’s first hardware device. These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components. The court gave OpenAI five days to turn over materials it has already collected and 14 days for any other materials related to this request, agreeing with Apple that these documents should be expedited. The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone — or smartphones more generally — if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers’ lives and how they engage with software and services. In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data. Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations. U.S. District Judge Edward Davila didn’t greenlight all of Apple’s requests for expedited access to OpenAI documents and messages relevant to the case. But he did rule that Apple could access the interview materials, alongside private LINE messages (from a messaging app) between individuals named in the case, including OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng. The judge also approved depositions for Liu and Peng, along with a third individual, OpenAI’s chief hardware officer, Tang Yew Tan. All three are former Apple employees. However, the judge denied Apple’s request to expedite its access to OpenAI’s research and development in specific areas, like metal finishes and power management. He also denied several of Apple’s broader discovery requests, like access to OpenAI’s hardware research or information about what its former employees created while working at OpenAI. That denial isn’t final, though; the judge left the door open for Apple to narrow its requests and try again. extraction.body: A federal judge on October 13, 2026 granted Apple limited expedited discovery in its trade-secret lawsuit against OpenAI, ordering the defendants to produce forensic device images, materials used to interview Apple job candidates, and private messages between two figures in the dispute. Judge Edward J. Davila of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California granted in part Apple’s motion in Apple Inc. v. Liu , the San Jose case naming former Apple employees Chang Liu and Tang Yew Tan, OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC, and io Products LLC. The defendants must respond to three document requests within 14 days, or within 5 days for materials already collected in the litigation. The first request covers all forensic images the defendants have collected in connection with the subject matter of Apple’s claims, including images identified in exhibits to the August 31, 2026 and September 11, 2026 declarations of Andrew Crain, or otherwise relied on by Crain. The second request, as modified by the court, requires production of all documents used to guide or conduct interviews of candidates from Apple for OpenAI’s Consumer Hardware Products Group (including its Consumer Hardware Product Group and Robotics Group), including checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts. Also covered are Technical Deep Dive presentations or other technical presentations summarizing or memorializing the content of those interviews with Apple employees, or any reference to Apple technology or parts. The third request requires Liu to produce all conversations on the LINE messaging app between him and Yu-Ting (“Alyssa”) Peng since January 1, 2026, including the conversations containing the messages cited in Liu’s August 31, 2026 declaration and its attached exhibit. Davila granted Apple the depositions of Liu, Tan, and Peng, to occur within 30 days after Apple receives all responses to the permitted requests. He also granted a corporate-designee deposition of OpenAI Foundation (formerly OpenAI, Inc.), OpenAI Group PBC, and io Products LLC (formerly io Products, Inc.) on the positions, roles, and responsibilities within OpenAI of the designated witnesses, Tan, Liu, Peng, and a redacted individual, subject to the same 30-day window. The court denied expedited treatment of Apple’s request for all documents related to OpenAI research and development on metal finishes, power management, or battery functionality for consumer hardware products, finding it better suited to ordinary merits discovery. It also denied, for now, Apple’s request to depose a fourth individual listed in its narrowed requests. Davila deferred ruling on all requests and deposition topics incorporating the term “Apple Originated Information,” which he found amorphous as currently defined. If Apple intends to pursue those requests, it must confer with the defendants and submit a more tailored definition within five days for the court to evaluate. The judge declined to hold that the permitted depositions come in addition to the deposition limits in the federal rules, writing that the court will entertain future motions to exceed those limits as necessary. Finding the motion suitable for disposition without oral argument under the district’s local rules, he vacated the hearing that had been scheduled for October 14, 2026. Apple filed its complaint on July 10, 2026, and the case was reassigned to Davila on July 23, 2026, according to the case docket . The complaint alleges trade secret misappropriation under the Defend Trade Secrets Act, the federal trade-secret statute, and breach of the individual defendants’ Intellectual Property Agreements. As recited in the ruling, Apple alleges that an investigation uncovered a pattern of trade secret theft by former Apple employees now working at OpenAI, including use of Apple’s proprietary information to assist OpenAI’s hardware development, to gain insider knowledge during interviews of Apple employees considering jobs at OpenAI, and to instruct new OpenAI hires on avoiding scrutiny when they leave Apple. Apple further alleges the corporate defendants acted in concert as an enterprise exploiting its confidential information to advance OpenAI’s efforts to enter the consumer hardware market. Apple sought expedited discovery on August 4, 2026, after moving for a preliminary injunction on August 3, 2026. The defendants opposed the discovery motion on August 18, Apple replied on August 25, and Apple filed a supplemental brief on August 31 presenting its forensic expert’s review of Liu’s MacBook, to which the defendants responded September 11 with their own expert’s findings, the docket entries show. After a September 14 status conference, the parties filed a joint submission containing Apple’s narrowed requests on September 18, 2026. The order applies the Ninth Circuit’s good-cause standard, which weighs whether a preliminary injunction is pending, the breadth of the requests, their purpose, the burden of compliance, and how far in advance of the typical discovery process the request came. On the first factor, the court agreed with Apple that because forensic images of Liu’s devices had become a prominent component of the pending preliminary-injunction motion, at least some of the requested discovery bore a clear relationship to that motion. It rejected the defendants’ argument, built on Liu’s January 2026 departure from Apple, that Apple’s delay in seeking relief alone justified denial. On breadth and burden, the court found the narrowed requests remained broad, pointing to the “Apple Originated Information” definition and the research-and-development request. It agreed with the defendants that some requests were sweeping enough that their suggestion that Apple meant to rummage through a competitor’s files was not entirely frivolous, while noting Apple had already supplied a preliminary trade-secret identification. The order recounts the parties’ competing forensic positions without weighing them at this stage: Apple’s expert concluded Liu used an Apple trade-secret file in March 2026 and told Peng in June 2026 to have Apple-issued devices restored and to start using them more, while the defendants’ expert found no evidence Liu used the file in connection with any AI platform, and the defendants stressed that Apple does not argue anything was actually deleted or restored. The court credited Apple’s position that forensic artifacts such as logs, metadata, and usage records are transient and at risk of loss, and agreed early discovery is needed to uncover the scope of any alleged misappropriation, quoting the joint submission’s warning that the alleged secrets could become “so deeply entangled with OpenAI’s hardware products or other research and development efforts that the harm cannot be undone.” The court found the request was not made significantly in advance of the typical discovery process and concluded that good cause supported granting a more limited version of Apple’s narrowed requests. coreStoryFacts.text: Apple said in its lawsuit that, because OpenAI's "misconduct is normalized and exemplified by leadership" its "nascent hardware business now rests on the shakiest of foundations, rotten to its core by its illegal reliance on misappropriated trade secrets".

In a federal lawsuit filed on Friday, Apple sued the artificial intelligence (AI) company, two of its employees, as well as io Products, claiming it has engaged in "a pattern of theft" of Apple's confidential product development and related work.
Drew Pusateri, a spokesman for OpenAI, told the BBC: "We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets."

Through these former employees and their access to "sensitive projects, trusted partner relationships, proprietary manufacturing techniques, and unreleased products," Apple claims OpenAI has been able to glean details of its product plans and operations.
Apple added that when OpenAI interviews current Apple employees for potential jobs the company allegedly tries to extract further information from them.

It is also suing Chang Liu, a senior electrical engineer who worked at Apple for eight years, and Tang Yew Tan, a vice president of design for iPhone and Apple Watch who spent 24 years with the company.
At least two long-time Apple workers who left the company to join OpenAI allegedly took part in this pattern by, in part, emailing themselves internal Apple information.
OpenAI interviewers allegedly have told the prospective hires to "bring 'actual parts' as 'props' from Apple for 'show and tell'" during their interview.
Apple has asked the court to immediately prohibit OpenAI from obtaining or using any alleged confidential information and it is seeking unspecified monetary damages.
It represents a major shift in relations between Apple and OpenAI, creator of the popular AI chatbot ChatGPT.
Yet, when Cook revealed in April that he was stepping down, Sam Altman, co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, publicly praised him as "a legend", adding he was "very thankful for everything he has done".
Tim Cook, Apple's outgoing CEO, had added ChatGPT into Apple devices as the company was looking to offer more AI features.
This year, Apple shifted more of its AI features to run on Google's Gemini model and tools.
OpenAI is expected to release its first hardware product, a type of keyboard to be used with its AI tools, this month.
The company also said that it had attempted to discuss it's concerns with OpenAI in February, but was ultimately ignored.
Apple filed a lawsuit against OpenAI on Friday alleging the artificial intelligence firm stole company trade secrets in a move to create its own hardware device.
“OpenAI’s nascent hardware business now rests on the shakiest of foundations, rotten to its core by its illegal reliance on misappropriated trade secrets,” Apple wrote in its complaint.
Tang Yew Tan, OpenAI’s chief hardware officer and a former vice-president at Apple, is named in the suit.
Apple alleges that Tan took information about Apple suppliers with him to OpenAI and encouraged interviewees at OpenAI to divulge confidential company information.

“Recently, significant evidence has emerged suggesting individuals employed by OpenAI wrongfully took Apple’s secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes and products,” an Apple spokesperson said in an email.
Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company was reviewing the court filing.
“We have no interest in other companies’ trade secrets,” he added.
“We remain focused on building innovative technology that empowers people everywhere.”
Apple’s lawsuit is a sharp turnaround for the two tech giants, which announced a major partnership in 2024.

Through these former employees and their access to "sensitive projects, trusted partner relationships, proprietary manufacturing techniques, and unreleased products," Apple claims OpenAI has been able to glean details of its product plans and operations. Apple added that when OpenAI interviews current Apple employees for potential jobs the company allegedly tries to extract further information from them. It is also suing Chang Liu, a senior electrical engineer who worked at Apple for eight years, and Tang Yew Tan, a vice president of design for iPhone and Apple Watch who spent 24 years with the company. At least two long-time Apple workers who left the company to join OpenAI allegedly took part in this pattern by, in part, emailing themselves internal Apple information. OpenAI interviewers allegedly have told the prospective hires to "bring 'actual parts' as 'props' from Apple for 'show and tell'" during their interview. Apple has asked the court to immediately prohibit OpenAI from obtaining or using any alleged confidential information and it is seeking unspecified monetary damages. It represents a major shift in relations between Apple and OpenAI, creator of the popular AI chatbot ChatGPT. Yet, when Cook revealed in April that he was stepping down, Sam Altman, co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, publicly praised him as "a legend", adding he was "very thankful for everything he has done". Tim Cook, Apple's outgoing CEO, had added ChatGPT into Apple devices as the company was looking to offer more AI features. This year, Apple shifted more of its AI features to run on Google's Gemini model and tools. OpenAI is expected to release its first hardware product, a type of keyboard to be used with its AI tools, this month. The company also said that it had attempted to discuss it's concerns with OpenAI in February, but was ultimately ignored.

sources.title: Apple sues OpenAI, alleging artificial intelligence company stole trade secrets - The Guardian
passages: Apple filed a lawsuit against OpenAI on Friday alleging the artificial intelligence firm stole company trade secrets in a move to create its own hardware device.
“OpenAI’s nascent hardware business now rests on the shakiest of foundations, rotten to its core by its illegal reliance on misappropriated trade secrets,” Apple wrote in its complaint.
Tang Yew Tan, OpenAI’s chief hardware officer and a former vice-president at Apple, is named in the suit.
Apple alleges that Tan took information about Apple suppliers with him to OpenAI and encouraged interviewees at OpenAI to divulge confidential company information.

“Recently, significant evidence has emerged suggesting individuals employed by OpenAI wrongfully took Apple’s secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes and products,” an Apple spokesperson said in an email.
Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company was reviewing the court filing.
“We have no interest in other companies’ trade secrets,” he added.
“We remain focused on building innovative technology that empowers people everywhere.”
Apple’s lawsuit is a sharp turnaround for the two tech giants, which announced a major partnership in 2024.
That deal involved Apple integrating OpenAI’s chatbot, ChatGPT, into the operating systems for iPhones, iPads and Macs.
But when Apple showcased its revamped voice assistant Siri last month, its AI component was based on Google’s Gemini AI model, rather than ChatGPT.

Tensions between the two companies began to simmer last year when OpenAI spent $6.4bn to acquire a hardware startup founded by former Apple design guru Jony Ive, indicating that the AI titan was foraying into hardware.
The company is seeking damages and a court order that would block OpenAI from possessing or using its trade secrets.
The suit claims OpenAI poached Apple employees, coaxing them to hand over confidential material, product designs and other tightly held information.

“He has directed job candidates still working for Apple to bring ‘actual parts’ from Apple to their interviews for ‘show and tell’ sessions in which he and his team at OpenAI can elicit still more Apple confidential information,” reads Apple’s complaint.

The suit claims OpenAI poached Apple employees, coaxing them to hand over confidential material, product designs and other tightly held information.

“Recently, significant evidence has emerged suggesting individuals employed by OpenAI wrongfully took Apple’s secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes and products,” an Apple spokesperson said in an email.

Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company was reviewing the court filing. “We have no interest in other companies’ trade secrets,” he added. “We remain focused on building innovative technology that empowers people everywhere.”

Apple’s lawsuit is a sharp turnaround for the two tech giants, which announced a major partnership in 2024. That deal involved Apple integrating OpenAI’s chatbot, ChatGPT, into the operating systems for iPhones, iPads and Macs. But when Apple showcased its revamped voice assistant Siri last month, its AI component was based on Google’s Gemini AI model, rather than ChatGPT.

Tensions between the two companies began to simmer last year when OpenAI spent $6.4bn to acquire a hardware startup founded by former Apple design guru Jony Ive, indicating that the AI titan was foraying into hardware. Ive’s startup, io Products, is also named in Apple’s lawsuit.
“OpenAI’s nascent hardware business now rests on the shakiest of foundations, rotten to its core by its illegal reliance on misappropriated trade secrets,” Apple wrote in its complaint.

The suit alleges several former Apple employees joined OpenAI, taking company trade secrets with them. Tang Yew Tan, OpenAI’s chief hardware officer and a former vice-president at Apple, is named in the suit. Apple alleges that Tan took information about Apple suppliers with him to OpenAI and encouraged interviewees at OpenAI to divulge confidential company information.

“He has directed job candidates still working for Apple to bring ‘actual parts’ from Apple to their interviews for ‘show and tell’ sessions in which he and his team at OpenAI can elicit still more Apple confidential information,” reads Apple’s complaint.

Chang Liu, another former Apple employee named in the suit who was hired at OpenAI, is accused of taking an Apple laptop with him when he left. Apple alleges that Liu used an authentication bug to breach the company’s internal network and downloaded “dozens of Apple’s confidential hardware-related files”.

The Apple spokesperson said: “Our teams are constantly developing breakthrough technologies to create the best products and services in the world, and protecting their work and intellectual property is something we take very seriously.”
The company is seeking damages and a court order that would block OpenAI from possessing or using its trade secrets.

sources.title: Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring records in Apple trade secrets case
passages: A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI’s hiring materials in the trade secrets-focused lawsuit the iPhone maker filed against OpenAI in July.

The court gave OpenAI five days to turn over materials it has already collected and 14 days for any other materials related to this request, agreeing with Apple that these documents should be expedited.

In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data.
Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations.

The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone — or smartphones more generally — if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers’ lives and how they engage with software and services.
That denial isn’t final, though; the judge left the door open for Apple to narrow its requests and try again.

These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components.

extraction.body: A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI’s hiring materials in the trade secrets-focused lawsuit the iPhone maker filed against OpenAI in July. Specifically, the court will allow Apple to view documents associated with OpenAI’s interviews with former Apple employees who applied for roles within its consumer hardware and robotics groups ahead of the rumored launch of OpenAI’s first hardware device. These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components. The court gave OpenAI five days to turn over materials it has already collected and 14 days for any other materials related to this request, agreeing with Apple that these documents should be expedited. The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone — or smartphones more generally — if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers’ lives and how they engage with software and services. In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data. Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations. U.S. District Judge Edward Davila didn’t greenlight all of Apple’s requests for expedited access to OpenAI documents and messages relevant to the case. But he did rule that Apple could access the interview materials, alongside private LINE messages (from a messaging app) between individuals named in the case, including OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng. The judge also approved depositions for Liu and Peng, along with a third individual, OpenAI’s chief hardware officer, Tang Yew Tan. All three are former Apple employees. However, the judge denied Apple’s request to expedite its access to OpenAI’s research and development in specific areas, like metal finishes and power management. He also denied several of Apple’s broader discovery requests, like access to OpenAI’s hardware research or information about what its former employees created while working at OpenAI. That denial isn’t final, though; the judge left the door open for Apple to narrow its requests and try again. In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data.
Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations.

The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone — or smartphones more generally — if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers’ lives and how they engage with software and services.
That denial isn’t final, though; the judge left the door open for Apple to narrow its requests and try again.

These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components.

extraction.body: A federal judge on October 13, 2026 granted Apple limited expedited discovery in its trade-secret lawsuit against OpenAI, ordering the defendants to produce forensic device images, materials used to interview Apple job candidates, and private messages between two figures in the dispute. Judge Edward J. Davila of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California granted in part Apple’s motion in Apple Inc. v. Liu , the San Jose case naming former Apple employees Chang Liu and Tang Yew Tan, OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC, and io Products LLC. The defendants must respond to three document requests within 14 days, or within 5 days for materials already collected in the litigation. The first request covers all forensic images the defendants have collected in connection with the subject matter of Apple’s claims, including images identified in exhibits to the August 31, 2026 and September 11, 2026 declarations of Andrew Crain, or otherwise relied on by Crain. The second request, as modified by the court, requires production of all documents used to guide or conduct interviews of candidates from Apple for OpenAI’s Consumer Hardware Products Group (including its Consumer Hardware Product Group and Robotics Group), including checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts. Also covered are Technical Deep Dive presentations or other technical presentations summarizing or memorializing the content of those interviews with Apple employees, or any reference to Apple technology or parts. The third request requires Liu to produce all conversations on the LINE messaging app between him and Yu-Ting (“Alyssa”) Peng since January 1, 2026, including the conversations containing the messages cited in Liu’s August 31, 2026 declaration and its attached exhibit. Davila granted Apple the depositions of Liu, Tan, and Peng, to occur within 30 days after Apple receives all responses to the permitted requests. He also granted a corporate-designee deposition of OpenAI Foundation (formerly OpenAI, Inc.), OpenAI Group PBC, and io Products LLC (formerly io Products, Inc.) on the positions, roles, and responsibilities within OpenAI of the designated witnesses, Tan, Liu, Peng, and a redacted individual, subject to the same 30-day window. The court denied expedited treatment of Apple’s request for all documents related to OpenAI research and development on metal finishes, power management, or battery functionality for consumer hardware products, finding it better suited to ordinary merits discovery. It also denied, for now, Apple’s request to depose a fourth individual listed in its narrowed requests. Davila deferred ruling on all requests and deposition topics incorporating the term “Apple Originated Information,” which he found amorphous as currently defined. If Apple intends to pursue those requests, it must confer with the defendants and submit a more tailored definition within five days for the court to evaluate. The judge declined to hold that the permitted depositions come in addition to the deposition limits in the federal rules, writing that the court will entertain future motions to exceed those limits as necessary. Finding the motion suitable for disposition without oral argument under the district’s local rules, he vacated the hearing that had been scheduled for October 14, 2026. Apple filed its complaint on July 10, 2026, and the case was reassigned to Davila on July 23, 2026, according to the case docket . The complaint alleges trade secret misappropriation under the Defend Trade Secrets Act, the federal trade-secret statute, and breach of the individual defendants’ Intellectual Property Agreements. As recited in the ruling, Apple alleges that an investigation uncovered a pattern of trade secret theft by former Apple employees now working at OpenAI, including use of Apple’s proprietary information to assist OpenAI’s hardware development, to gain insider knowledge during interviews of Apple employees considering jobs at OpenAI, and to instruct new OpenAI hires on avoiding scrutiny when they leave Apple. Apple further alleges the corporate defendants acted in concert as an enterprise exploiting its confidential information to advance OpenAI’s efforts to enter the consumer hardware market. Apple sought expedited discovery on August 4, 2026, after moving for a preliminary injunction on August 3, 2026. The defendants opposed the discovery motion on August 18, Apple replied on August 25, and Apple filed a supplemental brief on August 31 presenting its forensic expert’s review of Liu’s MacBook, to which the defendants responded September 11 with their own expert’s findings, the docket entries show. After a September 14 status conference, the parties filed a joint submission containing Apple’s narrowed requests on September 18, 2026. The order applies the Ninth Circuit’s good-cause standard, which weighs whether a preliminary injunction is pending, the breadth of the requests, their purpose, the burden of compliance, and how far in advance of the typical discovery process the request came. On the first factor, the court agreed with Apple that because forensic images of Liu’s devices had become a prominent component of the pending preliminary-injunction motion, at least some of the requested discovery bore a clear relationship to that motion. It rejected the defendants’ argument, built on Liu’s January 2026 departure from Apple, that Apple’s delay in seeking relief alone justified denial. On breadth and burden, the court found the narrowed requests remained broad, pointing to the “Apple Originated Information” definition and the research-and-development request. It agreed with the defendants that some requests were sweeping enough that their suggestion that Apple meant to rummage through a competitor’s files was not entirely frivolous, while noting Apple had already supplied a preliminary trade-secret identification. The order recounts the parties’ competing forensic positions without weighing them at this stage: Apple’s expert concluded Liu used an Apple trade-secret file in March 2026 and told Peng in June 2026 to have Apple-issued devices restored and to start using them more, while the defendants’ expert found no evidence Liu used the file in connection with any AI platform, and the defendants stressed that Apple does not argue anything was actually deleted or restored. The court credited Apple’s position that forensic artifacts such as logs, metadata, and usage records are transient and at risk of loss, and agreed early discovery is needed to uncover the scope of any alleged misappropriation, quoting the joint submission’s warning that the alleged secrets could become “so deeply entangled with OpenAI’s hardware products or other research and development efforts that the harm cannot be undone.” The court found the request was not made significantly in advance of the typical discovery process and concluded that good cause supported granting a more limited version of Apple’s narrowed requests. sources.title: Google Play adding ‘personal library’ to access your vibe-coded Android apps - 9to5Google
passages: The biggest update is Google Play’s embrace of vibe-coded Android apps.
Since May , Google AI Studio has allowed you to generate Android apps and quickly deploy them to your phone using ADB.
Google is now going a step further by letting you “launch personal apps on your own device” via the Play Store.
A “Your personal library” section allows you to access apps across multiple devices for an easy restore and install experience.
Elsewhere, Google Play is expanding Sports Topic Pages that show live scores and compatible streaming apps to the Premier League, Champions League, La Liga, Liga MX, and Major League Soccer.
Ask Play can now generate app comparisons that highlight “key differences and user sentiment.”
In the future, Google Play will let you “graduate to a professional developer account with the same Trust & Safety reviews and high-quality standards.”
Google today announced a slew of Play Store updates across vibe-coding, game discovery, social features, and more.

The biggest update is Google Play’s embrace of vibe-coded Android apps. Since May , Google AI Studio has allowed you to generate Android apps and quickly deploy them to your phone using ADB. Google is now going a step further by letting you “launch personal apps on your own device” via the Play Store. A “Your personal library” section allows you to access apps across multiple devices for an easy restore and install experience. This is rolling out starting today in the US and other select markets. The Play Store will soon let you privately share your apps with select users. These generated Android apps are kept “secure, private, and separate from the public store catalog.” It’s intended for small-scale sharing, with these apps going through a security review. Plus, see how players with similar Gamer DNA are engaging with a title, find out how many people you follow are playing it, read user review summaries and learn which games are trending and why. This will be joined by Game Playlists that let you curate and soon share a collection of titles. The Play Store is boosting social competitions with Sprints, or “high-energy, 48-hour micro-challenges” that involve matching with groups of two to five players for “fast-paced contests.” The Sidekick in-game overlay is also adding “30-second Playback” clips for sharing. Elsewhere, Google Play is expanding Sports Topic Pages that show live scores and compatible streaming apps to the Premier League, Champions League, La Liga, Liga MX, and Major League Soccer. sources.title: Google lets you make personal Android apps for free now – with just prompts - ZDNET
passages: Are you tired of ad overload in free, single-task apps?
Or, can you not find an app that fits a weirdly specific need?
Now you can make custom apps for your own Android phone, even if you have zero coding experience.
One Tuesday, Google announced that anyone with a standard Google account can build personal apps in Google AI Studio.
These apps will run on your own device, launched from a private part of Google Play, and won’t be included in the public Play Store.
You’ll be able to share your apps with close family and friends in the coming months, but you don’t have to.
Custom Android apps make app development a much more personal and potentially user-friendly experience.

extraction.body: Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private. These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator. The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android. Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use. These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android. Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up. “That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.” In the months ahead, the company said that users will be able to share their vibe-coded creations with a network of trusted friends. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child’s T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store. And if the app ever really becomes popular, there will be a way to shift the personal app to one that’s published on the Google Play Store for everyone to try, after completing the trust and safety reviews. Google will also allow users to curate their own lists of games, post questions about games to a new Community Posts section, and join new 48-hour gaming challenges called Sprints, among other gaming-related feature updates. Plus, the Play Store’s built-in AI assistant, Ask Play, is being updated to offer comparisons, allowing users to see the key differences between similar applications. Google Play apps and games will also be more deeply integrated into Gemini’s conversations. The changes are rolling out alongside Google Play’s new support for an age-range feature that allows parents to share their child’s age range, but not their exact birthdate, with developers to get an age-appropriate experience. sources.title: Google Play Vibe Coding Lets Users Build Private Android Apps - Innovation Village
passages: Google Play vibe-coded apps can now run privately on Android devices, allowing users to create personal software with artificial intelligence without publishing it to the public Play Store.
The change is significant, but it does not mean Google is abandoning its control over Android distribution.
Personal apps must still comply with Google Play’s existing policies.
Announced on Tuesday, October 13, the feature connects apps created through Google AI Studio with users’ Android devices.
Instead of opening a paid developer account and publishing an app for a public audience, users can launch their creations through a standard Google account.
Google plans to introduce secure sharing with selected friends and family in the coming months, giving users another option between keeping an app personal and releasing it publicly.
For Google, that pathway could encourage more people to build within its ecosystem rather than relying on alternative installation methods.
It also keeps Google Play relevant as AI makes software creation easier and competition over app distribution increases.
Google is also updating how users discover applications and games.
Its Game Finder feature uses personal gaming preferences to recommend titles, while Ask Play is gaining comparison tools to help users evaluate similar apps.
The strategic question is whether the Play Store can evolve from a marketplace for finished products into infrastructure for software that users create themselves.
Traditional app development generally requires developers to anticipate the needs of a broad audience and build products that can serve enough users to justify the investment.
This is the promise of vibe coding: people can describe what they want in natural language and allow AI to generate much of the underlying code.
The next stage will depend on whether users can move beyond novelty projects to build applications they genuinely rely on.
If that happens, the future of mobile software may be defined not only by the apps available to everyone, but also by the ones individuals can build for themselves.
As AI tools make coding more accessible, applications no longer need to be designed for millions of users to be useful.

extraction.body: Google Play vibe-coded apps can now run privately on Android devices, allowing users to create personal software with artificial intelligence without publishing it to the public Play Store. The new feature from Google makes it easier for people to turn everyday needs into custom applications, even without traditional programming skills. Announced on Tuesday, October 13, the feature connects apps created through Google AI Studio with users’ Android devices. Instead of opening a paid developer account and publishing an app for a public audience, users can launch their creations through a standard Google account. Initially, the feature is rolling out to adults aged 18 and older in the United States and select markets. These apps will remain private, absent from public Play Store search results and accessible only to their creators. Google plans to introduce secure sharing with selected friends and family in the coming months, giving users another option between keeping an app personal and releasing it publicly. The update reflects a broader change in software development. As AI tools make coding more accessible, applications no longer need to be designed for millions of users to be useful. They can be built for one person, one household or a specific problem that existing software does not adequately address. Until now, people experimenting with AI-generated Android applications faced a gap between creating an app and conveniently using it on their own devices. They could build web applications or work through more technical installation processes, but distributing a native Android app through Google Play traditionally required a developer account and additional publishing steps. Google’s new feature simplifies that process. Users can describe an idea to Gemini through Google AI Studio, refine the generated application and launch it for personal use. The potential applications are straightforward. Someone could create a specialised expense tracker that matches their budgeting habits, a personalised workout log or a household organiser tailored to their family. A student could build a revision tool around a particular subject, while a small business owner could experiment with a simple inventory application. These tools do not need to compete with established apps or attract thousands of downloads. Their value comes from solving a specific problem for the person who created them. This is the promise of vibe coding: people can describe what they want in natural language and allow AI to generate much of the underlying code. It does not eliminate the need to test software or understand its limitations, but it lowers the technical barrier to experimentation. The change is significant, but it does not mean Google is abandoning its control over Android distribution. Personal apps must still comply with Google Play’s existing policies. Users who want to distribute their creations publicly must move to a professional developer account and pass the platform’s standard trust and safety reviews. This creates a clearer path from experimentation to publication. A personal project can begin as a private tool, be shared with a small group and eventually become a public product if it proves useful. For Google, that pathway could encourage more people to build within its ecosystem rather than relying on alternative installation methods. It also keeps Google Play relevant as AI makes software creation easier and competition over app distribution increases. The strategic question is whether the Play Store can evolve from a marketplace for finished products into infrastructure for software that users create themselves. Google is effectively moving beyond the idea that every useful application must first become a conventional public product. However, the distinction between personal and public apps remains important. An app generated for individual use may contain bugs, mishandle information or produce unreliable results. Private distribution does not automatically make software secure or accurate. Users will still need to be cautious about the permissions they grant and the information they enter. Google is also updating how users discover applications and games. Its Game Finder feature uses personal gaming preferences to recommend titles, while Ask Play is gaining comparison tools to help users evaluate similar apps. Google is also bringing Play Store app links into Gemini conversations, allowing the assistant to surface relevant applications directly. Together, these changes show how Google is adapting the Play Store for an environment increasingly shaped by AI. The technology is influencing not only how software is built, but also how people find, personalise and use it. The larger opportunity is a shift away from one-size-fits-all software. Traditional app development generally requires developers to anticipate the needs of a broad audience and build products that can serve enough users to justify the investment. AI-generated personal apps could address smaller, more specific needs that commercial developers have little incentive to pursue. Yet creating software cheaply does not guarantee that it will work well. As more people generate applications, testing, maintenance, privacy and security will become increasingly important. Users may be able to create their own solutions, but they will still need ways to recognise when those solutions are unreliable. Google’s new feature is an early step towards that more personal software environment. It does not replace professional development or remove the need for platform oversight. Instead, it makes the space between having an idea and using a working Android app considerably smaller. The next stage will depend on whether users can move beyond novelty projects to build applications they genuinely rely on. If that happens, the future of mobile software may be defined not only by the apps available to everyone, but also by the ones individuals can build for themselves. A writer exploring the intersections of innovation, culture and fashion across Africa

extraction.body: Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private. These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator. The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android. Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use. These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android. Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up. “That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.” In the months ahead, the company said that users will be able to share their vibe-coded creations with a network of trusted friends. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child’s T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store. And if the app ever really becomes popular, there will be a way to shift the personal app to one that’s published on the Google Play Store for everyone to try, after completing the trust and safety reviews. Google will also allow users to curate their own lists of games, post questions about games to a new Community Posts section, and join new 48-hour gaming challenges called Sprints, among other gaming-related feature updates. Plus, the Play Store’s built-in AI assistant, Ask Play, is being updated to offer comparisons, allowing users to see the key differences between similar applications. Google Play apps and games will also be more deeply integrated into Gemini’s conversations. The changes are rolling out alongside Google Play’s new support for an age-range feature that allows parents to share their child’s age range, but not their exact birthdate, with developers to get an age-appropriate experience. sources.title: Google Play Vibe Coding Lets Users Build Private Android Apps - Innovation Village
passages: Google Play vibe-coded apps can now run privately on Android devices, allowing users to create personal software with artificial intelligence without publishing it to the public Play Store.
The change is significant, but it does not mean Google is abandoning its control over Android distribution.
Personal apps must still comply with Google Play’s existing policies.
Announced on Tuesday, October 13, the feature connects apps created through Google AI Studio with users’ Android devices.
Instead of opening a paid developer account and publishing an app for a public audience, users can launch their creations through a standard Google account.
Google plans to introduce secure sharing with selected friends and family in the coming months, giving users another option between keeping an app personal and releasing it publicly.
For Google, that pathway could encourage more people to build within its ecosystem rather than relying on alternative installation methods.
It also keeps Google Play relevant as AI makes software creation easier and competition over app distribution increases.
Google is also updating how users discover applications and games.
Its Game Finder feature uses personal gaming preferences to recommend titles, while Ask Play is gaining comparison tools to help users evaluate similar apps.
The strategic question is whether the Play Store can evolve from a marketplace for finished products into infrastructure for software that users create themselves.
Traditional app development generally requires developers to anticipate the needs of a broad audience and build products that can serve enough users to justify the investment.
This is the promise of vibe coding: people can describe what they want in natural language and allow AI to generate much of the underlying code.
The next stage will depend on whether users can move beyond novelty projects to build applications they genuinely rely on.
If that happens, the future of mobile software may be defined not only by the apps available to everyone, but also by the ones individuals can build for themselves.
As AI tools make coding more accessible, applications no longer need to be designed for millions of users to be useful.

extraction.body: Google Play vibe-coded apps can now run privately on Android devices, allowing users to create personal software with artificial intelligence without publishing it to the public Play Store. The new feature from Google makes it easier for people to turn everyday needs into custom applications, even without traditional programming skills. Announced on Tuesday, October 13, the feature connects apps created through Google AI Studio with users’ Android devices. Instead of opening a paid developer account and publishing an app for a public audience, users can launch their creations through a standard Google account. Initially, the feature is rolling out to adults aged 18 and older in the United States and select markets. These apps will remain private, absent from public Play Store search results and accessible only to their creators. Google plans to introduce secure sharing with selected friends and family in the coming months, giving users another option between keeping an app personal and releasing it publicly. The update reflects a broader change in software development. As AI tools make coding more accessible, applications no longer need to be designed for millions of users to be useful. They can be built for one person, one household or a specific problem that existing software does not adequately address. Until now, people experimenting with AI-generated Android applications faced a gap between creating an app and conveniently using it on their own devices. They could build web applications or work through more technical installation processes, but distributing a native Android app through Google Play traditionally required a developer account and additional publishing steps. Google’s new feature simplifies that process. Users can describe an idea to Gemini through Google AI Studio, refine the generated application and launch it for personal use. The potential applications are straightforward. Someone could create a specialised expense tracker that matches their budgeting habits, a personalised workout log or a household organiser tailored to their family. A student could build a revision tool around a particular subject, while a small business owner could experiment with a simple inventory application. These tools do not need to compete with established apps or attract thousands of downloads. Their value comes from solving a specific problem for the person who created them. This is the promise of vibe coding: people can describe what they want in natural language and allow AI to generate much of the underlying code. It does not eliminate the need to test software or understand its limitations, but it lowers the technical barrier to experimentation. The change is significant, but it does not mean Google is abandoning its control over Android distribution. Personal apps must still comply with Google Play’s existing policies. Users who want to distribute their creations publicly must move to a professional developer account and pass the platform’s standard trust and safety reviews. This creates a clearer path from experimentation to publication. A personal project can begin as a private tool, be shared with a small group and eventually become a public product if it proves useful. For Google, that pathway could encourage more people to build within its ecosystem rather than relying on alternative installation methods. It also keeps Google Play relevant as AI makes software creation easier and competition over app distribution increases. The strategic question is whether the Play Store can evolve from a marketplace for finished products into infrastructure for software that users create themselves. Google is effectively moving beyond the idea that every useful application must first become a conventional public product. However, the distinction between personal and public apps remains important. An app generated for individual use may contain bugs, mishandle information or produce unreliable results. Private distribution does not automatically make software secure or accurate. Users will still need to be cautious about the permissions they grant and the information they enter. Google is also updating how users discover applications and games. Its Game Finder feature uses personal gaming preferences to recommend titles, while Ask Play is gaining comparison tools to help users evaluate similar apps. Google is also bringing Play Store app links into Gemini conversations, allowing the assistant to surface relevant applications directly. Together, these changes show how Google is adapting the Play Store for an environment increasingly shaped by AI. The technology is influencing not only how software is built, but also how people find, personalise and use it. The larger opportunity is a shift away from one-size-fits-all software. Traditional app development generally requires developers to anticipate the needs of a broad audience and build products that can serve enough users to justify the investment. AI-generated personal apps could address smaller, more specific needs that commercial developers have little incentive to pursue. Yet creating software cheaply does not guarantee that it will work well. As more people generate applications, testing, maintenance, privacy and security will become increasingly important. Users may be able to create their own solutions, but they will still need ways to recognise when those solutions are unreliable. Google’s new feature is an early step towards that more personal software environment. It does not replace professional development or remove the need for platform oversight. Instead, it makes the space between having an idea and using a working Android app considerably smaller. The next stage will depend on whether users can move beyond novelty projects to build applications they genuinely rely on. If that happens, the future of mobile software may be defined not only by the apps available to everyone, but also by the ones individuals can build for themselves. A writer exploring the intersections of innovation, culture and fashion across Africa

passages: 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Schneider Electric, a global energy technology leader, today announced a new Smart Thermostat, co-developed with Apple for Apple Home Collection, and an exclusive Power Mount for the newly announced Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted).
The products will be available within Schneider Electric's Schneider Home residential portfolio.
Users can adjust the temperature hands-free using Siri on Apple products.
The small metal bezel features a smooth silver finish, blending perfectly in any environment.
Its translucent display gives it a soft matte face with no glare, and proximity awareness makes every interaction effortless and gentle on the eyes in a dark room.
Built-in sensing plus optional Room Sensors allow the system to sense conditions including temperature and humidity, adapting to the unique needs of users' homes.
" The smartest home is one where every part works together, and that's only possible through technology that enables energy intelligence," said Olivier Blum, CEO of Schneider Electric.
All three Power Mounts feature precision magnets to securely hold Apple HomeView against the wall to stay powered.

For a seamless professional installation with no visible wires, the AC Wired Power Mount connects to electrical wiring through a single wall box, and the PoE Wired Power Mount receives power and data through a standard ethernet cable hidden in the wall.

" At Apple, our goal is to deliver great products that make everyday experiences simpler and more enjoyable, with privacy at the core, " said Matthew Costello, Apple's vice president of Hardware Engineering.

Set up, connectivity, and security have never been better, with effortless tap-to-pair NFC functionality even when Smart Thermostat is not powered, allowing set up in seconds by simply bringing an iPhone nearby.

Home energy is becoming more complex, benefiting from different sources of electricity, consuming more power, and operating in a siloed ecosystem across heating and cooling, water heating, EV charging, appliances, and connected devices.

Schneider Home brings energy intelligence to the home, with solutions including the Smart Thermostat, EV chargers, circuit breakers, electrical panels, uninterruptable power supply (UPS) and connected wiring devices.

Schneider Home represents a vision for how home energy technologies can work together with seamless orchestration, helping homeowners better understand, manage, and optimize their energy use, without compromising comfort, simplicity, or cost.

For customers who prefer to have their smart home accessories professionally installed, Apple Retail now offers third-party installation from ADT for an additional charge, available in the U.S. starting this fall.
ADT also leverages the nationwide installer network from Qmerit , backed by Schneider Electric.
Its technologies enable buildings, data centers, factories, infrastructure, and grids to operate as open, interconnected ecosystems, enhancing performance, resilience, and sustainability.
The portfolio includes intelligent devices, software-defined architectures, AI-powered systems, digital services, and expert advisory.
With 160,000 employees and 1 million partners in over 100 countries, Schneider Electric is consistently ranked among the world's most sustainable companies.
Smart Thermostat retails for a suggested MSRP of $199.99; Room Sensor retails for a suggested MSRP of $39.99.

passages: Meet Apple HomeView, a new way to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage the home

“It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home.

And it’s powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI at its core, drawing on personal context from your iPhone to help you find what you need and get more done, all while keeping everyone’s information private and secure.”

With a stunning 7-inch Liquid Retina display, HomeView brings entertainment, connection, and smart home management together in one place, from playing music and making FaceTime calls to home monitoring and hands-free automations with voice control — all designed with privacy and security at the core.
By setting up multiple HomeView, HomePod, HomePod mini, and AirPlay-compatible speakers around the house, users can enjoy music throughout the entire home with multiroom audio.

HomeView also works with Apple Home Collection — a new lineup of smart home cameras, thermostats, and a lock designed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric — as well as other Works with Apple Home and Matter accessories.
8 Together, they help users understand what’s happening inside and outside, manage access, keep the home at just the right temperature, and so much more.
With broad world knowledge, anyone in the home can ask Siri about virtually any topic and get an answer.
HomeView was built with the environment in mind and drives progress toward Apple’s ambitious plan to be carbon neutral across its entire footprint by 2030.

HomeView is made with 100 percent recycled aluminum in the enclosure base and in the enclosure of the wall-mounted model, 100 percent recycled gold plating and tin solder in all Apple-designed printed circuit boards, and 100 percent recycled rare earth elements in all magnets.
HomeView meets Apple’s high standards for energy efficiency and safe chemistry.
HomeView and the A18 chip include Secure Exclaves: protected and compartmentalized runtimes used to process camera and microphone data separately from the rest of the system.
Data that is processed and analyzed in Secure Exclaves cannot be accessed by the HomeView software, apps, the user, or Apple.

To ensure that personal content stays private to each individual, even when HomeView is shared by the whole household, content in apps like Messages and Calendar is only surfaced when the enrolled user is recognized by their face, and when their paired iPhone or iPad is present and has been recently unlocked.
Apple revolutionized personal technology with the introduction of the Macintosh in 1984.
Today, Apple leads the world in innovation with iPhone, iPad, Mac, AirPods, Apple Watch, and Apple Vision Pro.

Apple’s six software platforms — iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, visionOS, and tvOS — provide seamless experiences across all Apple devices and empower people with breakthrough services including the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Pay, iCloud, and Apple TV.
Apple’s more than 150,000 employees are dedicated to making the best products on earth and to leaving the world better than we found it.
HomeView offers an exceptional listening experience through a custom-engineered acoustic system.
Two custom full-range drivers in the display keep everything sounding crisp and clean while delivering room-filling Spatial Audio.
A down-firing woofer and two force-cancelling passive radiators are built into the base, offering incredible bass extension.
Siri requests on HomeView can use on-device processing or Private Cloud Compute, which extends the privacy of the device to the cloud.

HomeView allows users to securely control their smart home by touch or with just their voice using Siri AI — viewing camera feeds, adjusting the thermostat and lights, locking doors, or closing the blinds.

With a stunning 7-inch Liquid Retina display, HomeView brings entertainment, connection, and smart home management together in one place, from playing music and making FaceTime calls to home monitoring and hands-free automations with voice control — all designed with privacy and security at the core. 1 HomeView recognizes users by their faces, adapting so they can access their personal content in Messages, FaceTime, Calendar, Reminders, and Find My. HomeView features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri that’s profoundly more capable and conversational, with broad world knowledge that powers richer music discovery and onscreen awareness. When paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled device, it can also draw on a user’s personal context, such as their Calendar, Messages, and relevant information across their apps, to provide more helpful, personalized responses. 2 Designed to fit in any space, HomeView can be placed on a tabletop as the center of the home or wall-mounted to fit in spaces like the entryway or hallway. Pre-orders start today, with availability beginning November 13. “Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user,” said Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing. “It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home. And it’s powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI at its core, drawing on personal context from your iPhone to help you find what you need and get more done, all while keeping everyone’s information private and secure.” HomeView features a beautiful aluminum design with a 7-inch Liquid Retina display connected to a domed speaker base by a stainless steel hinge that provides a smooth tilt for comfortable viewing on tabletops of any height. The perfect addition to a kitchen counter, nightstand, or side table, HomeView comes in four beautiful colors — silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray — each finished with a matching cable. The elegant design and Liquid Retina display seamlessly blend into any space while remaining clearly visible from across the room. It features adaptive display technologies, including True Tone, that react to changing light throughout the day. Automatic brightness adjusts from 500 nits — bright enough to stay vivid and easy to see even in a sunlit room — down to just 0.3 nits, making it ideal for the nightstand. The HomeView interface intelligently adjusts based on the user’s distance, showing simpler information that’s viewable from across the room and richer detail as they step closer. A separate wall-mounted HomeView model — available in space gray and silver — offers the same 7-inch Liquid Retina display, powerful set of features, and rich audio. It can be attached to a wall using three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home, with options for self-installation or professional installation. A Personalized Experience for Each User in the Home HomeView recognizes up to six people and delivers a personalized experience for each one. Each user gets their own personalized Home Screen with apps and widgets. Personal content stays private from others, while shared photo albums and music can be easily enjoyed by everyone in a household, including guests. Featuring Siri AI, Powered by Apple Intelligence HomeView features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence and advanced Apple silicon. Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding and onscreen awareness. With broad world knowledge, anyone in the home can ask Siri about virtually any topic and get an answer. With an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, Siri AI does more for each person — taking action across apps and surfacing relevant information from Messages and Calendar, playlists on Apple Music, and more by drawing on their personal context. Users have the ability to customize the expressiveness and pace of Siri’s voice on their paired and compatible device so that it’s just right for them. That customization carries over to HomeView, allowing users to go back and forth with Siri in a conversation like never before. 3 Conversations that start on HomeView seamlessly continue in the Siri app, which uses iCloud to privately sync history across a user’s products, so they can pick up the conversation on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, or Apple Vision Pro. With Siri AI built into HomeView, even users without an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad will benefit from Siri AI’s broad world knowledge; ability to have rich, natural conversations; and improved music discovery. With powerful new features and unrivaled privacy protections, Siri remains the world’s most private digital assistant. Users can personalize HomeView with a collection of playful and informative faces that display information at a glance, taking full advantage of the vibrant Liquid Retina display. The Photos face brings cherished memories to life with stunning Portrait-style depth effects that keep the subject sharp while creating a beautifully blurred foreground and background. By selecting a shared album, users can turn HomeView into a living photo frame that loved ones near and far can help fill. The Flow face dynamically responds to physical presence and movement, transforming HomeView into a piece of interactive art. And even Snoopy comes to life on HomeView, with animations that reflect the time of day, the weather, sporting events, and holiday moments. HomeView offers an exceptional listening experience through a custom-engineered acoustic system. Two custom full-range drivers in the display keep everything sounding crisp and clean while delivering room-filling Spatial Audio. A down-firing woofer and two force-cancelling passive radiators are built into the base, offering incredible bass extension. Powered by Apple silicon and real-time system sensors, advanced computational audio continuously optimizes loudness and bass response at any volume. The wall-mounted version delivers rich sound with two custom drivers and computational audio tuned specifically for on-wall placement. HomeView is the perfect way to enjoy Apple Music, complete with animated album art and lyrics, as well as Apple Podcasts, Apple News, 4 Apple TV, and compatible third-party audio and video apps. 5 With Handoff, users can continue listening to a song they were playing in the car or on a walk by placing their iPhone in front of the HomeView display. Intercom lets users broadcast a quick message to a single room or the whole house — reaching other HomeView and HomePod speakers, as well as personal devices like iPhone, iPad, or Apple Watch.
