sources.title: Is iOS 15 Coming? Apple Music for Artists’ New Icon Reportedly a Preparation for New Software Version
passages: The iOS 15's presence may be speculation or in preparation for the new version of its operating system, as September draws near. iOS 15 Speculations Due to Apple Music for Artists Apple has recently announced and released the "Apple Music for Artists" version of the company's iTunes and in-device music player.

extraction.body: Apple has recently announced that it has updated the icon for its Apple Music, which would be intended for artists and song makers, who then could view their engagements and keep track of their statistics online. However, the change in the icon also led to raise speculations that a new software version for the iPhone is coming, and that is the iOS 15. While there are no updates or information regarding the iOS 15 as of this moment, this might be the earliest speculation or suspicion that Apple is already gearing up for the release of their next OS version. However, it would not be released anytime during this moment, especially as it could take up to a year since it last released the iOS 14 in September. Apple is known for observing a release of an update of their devices a year after its initial update has taken place, and this has been apparent with the iPhone 11 to iPhone 12 transition, which was even late by a month. The iOS 15's presence may be speculation or in preparation for the new version of its operating system, as September draws near. iOS 15 Speculations Due to Apple Music for Artists Apple has recently announced and released the "Apple Music for Artists" version of the company's iTunes and in-device music player. Apple Music for Artists LogoWith this new venture by Apple, they have also provided a new icon, which now sports a white background that has accents of red, used for the outline of the music note logo and the box itself. Apple may have used this chance to design a new logo so that people would not be confused between the Apple Music logo and the new venture dedicated to Artists.However, it was also due to this icon that led leakers and speculators to perceive this as the "something new" from Apple that suggests something is brewing up in their development team, concerned for the iOS. One of the indicators of an iOS change is the new look and appearance for logos of the built-in apps from Apple, and this might suggest it. Currently, there is no news regarding the arrival of the iOS 15 anytime soon, nor its features and functions once it officially releases to public beta testers and users for a first-hand look. However, according to Mac Rumors, what it does suggest is how the icons of the iOS 15 would look once it releases for the public in the coming months. The design of the Apple Music for Artists' logo shows that it would use the same looks like the old icons, but it would focus more on "popping up" the outlines of the design, which was a similar case to the iOS 14 transition. This article is owned by Tech TimesWritten by Isaiah Alonzo

(NASDAQ: FFR ), a U.S.-based Embodied AI ("EAI") robotics company that has proposed to acquire Faraday Future Intelligent Electric Inc.'s (NASDAQ: FFAI ) EAI Robotics business, today highlighted FFAI's announcement that this week's Investor Weekly Report from Faraday Future ("FF") Founder and Global CEO YT Jia has been rescheduled to October 14.

Additionally, FFR and FFAI will host a joint new product launch event on October 14, 2026, featuring four major launches focused on embodied AI robotics, Physical AI education, and developer enablement.
The event will feature FF Nova, FF's first embodied AI humanoid robot designed for developers and educational institutions, through an exclusive, invitation-only launch.
FFAI has also announced that FF will introduce FF Nova Mini, a humanoid robot designed for foundational Physical AI education, along with the EAI Education Ecosystem Brain and Curriculum Skills 2.0.
In addition, FF will launch the FF Nova Developer Reinforcement Learning Platform and open exclusive early access to the developer community.

FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem Inc. (NASDAQ: FFR ) is a U.S.-based Embodied AI (EAI) robotics company that is in the process of acquiring the FF EAI Robotics business. Upon completion of the acquisition, the Company will focus on the research and development, manufacturing, commercialization, and deployment of intelligent robotic technologies, products, and industry solutions.

The Company is committed to building a "Four-Core Full-Stack" AI ecosystem covering the full lifecycle of robotics, consisting of EAI Brain & Developer Platform, EAI Devices, Industry Productivity Solutions, and EAI Data Factory. Guided by the technology and product philosophy of "One Brain, Multi-forms, Multi-capabilities," the Company aims to empower humanoid, biomimetic, and other robotic form factors through a unified EAI Brain, while continuously expanding their multi-task and multi-scenario capabilities. The ecosystem is designed to support the full robotics lifecycle, including R&D, deployment, data collection and training, operations, and commercial applications.

The FF EAI Robotics business has already achieved commercial deliveries of humanoid and biomimetic robotic products. Through its multi-form-factor robotic products, EAI technology platform, closed-loop data capabilities, and industry solutions, the business continues to advance the scaled adoption of robotics across real-world applications. The Company also operates RoboShare, a robot-sharing and services platform designed to connect robotic assets, service capabilities, customer demand, and ecosystem partners, further strengthening its robotics commercialization and service ecosystem.

Shakur is considered one of the most influential and versatile rappers of all time and had a burgeoning film career as an actor at the time of his death. His legend has only grown since. His songs still resonate among fans with themes of hardship, love and Black struggles. The killing went unsolved for years until Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, gave interviews and published his role in the shooting in his 2019 tell-all memoir. He explained how Shakur and his entourage beat up Davis' nephew hours before the shooting in Las Vegas. He said he sought retaliation, and that he was in the passenger seat of the Cadillac and passed the gun to the backseat, where shots were fired. Davis had spoken to detectives years before but avoided prosecution because of an agreement he made with law enforcement. During the weekslong trial, prosecutors relied on Davis' own statements he made to law enforcement and documentarians. They argued Davis orchestrated the shooting and provided the gun used in Shakur's death, which was the result of a rivalry between the South Side Compton Crips and Mob Piru. Davis' defense attorney pointed to a lack of physical evidence that connected his client to the 30-year-old crime, and he portrayed Davis as a liar who was trying to make money. After nine days of hearing testimony in August, the jury deliberated for three hours before turning over the guilty verdict. Davis said in court that he plans to appeal. Shakur's family is expected to speak at the sentencing, including his siblings Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur and Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur. Following the verdict, prosecutor Binu Palal said that to many people, Shakur was an icon or an idea, "but to the family, Tupac Shakur was a brother, a son, a cousin, a loved person ripped from them 30 years ago.” Palal said the family had to sit through years of Davis “bragging about killing someone they loved.” "They loved that man. And the arrogance that Mr. Davis had in expressing his joy in killing that man ultimately was his undoing,” Palal said. Davis is the only person to be charged and convicted in the killing of Shakur. The three other people who allegedly were in the Cadillac — including Davis' nephew Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson who Davis said was the one who pulled the trigger — have died. Sean “Diddy” Combs and his alleged role were brought up often throughout the trial. Witnesses testified Combs used members of the South Side Compton Crips for security for Bad Boy Records. In his book and public statements, Davis alleged Combs offered him money to kill Shakur and Knight. Combs, who is serving a four-year prison sentence after being convicted of prostitution-related offenses, has repeatedly denied any involvement in the death of Shakur. Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson has said his office doesn't believe it has sufficient evidence to charge anyone else. “But like any other case, if we come into more information, more evidence, we can always consider filing additional charges,” he said following the guilty verdict. “But today, we don't believe that's the appropriate move to make.” Duane Davis, right, talks stands with his attorney Michael Sanft during a sentencing hearing after his murder conviction in the death of rapper Tupac Shakur on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Las Vegas. (AP Photo/John Locher, Pool) FILE - Mopreme Shakur leaves for recess following the closing arguments in the murder trial of Duane Davis, Aug. 31, 2026, in Las Vegas. (AP Photo/Lucas Peltier, File) FILE - Duane Davis, right, and his attorney Michael Sanft sit in a courtroom, after a jury found Davis guilty of first-degree murder in his trial related to the 1996 killing of rapper Tupac Shakur, at Clark County District Court Regional Justice Center on Aug. 31, 2026, in Las Vegas. (Bizuayehu Tesfaye/Las Vegas Review-Journal via AP, Pool)

(NASDAQ: FFAI) (“Faraday Future,” “FF” or the “Company”), a California-based global Embodied AI (EAI) ecosystem company, today announced a long-term employee equity incentive plan at its robotics subsidiary, FF EAI Robotics Inc. (“FFR”). FF EAI Robotics is allocating approximately 25% of the capitalization of FF EAI Robotics on a fully diluted basis as the 2026 Equity Incentive Plan to provide long-term equity incentives for the Company’s core management team, key leaders, and key employees. Such equity of FFR is not convertible to equity of FFAI. “The equity incentive plan is intended to create a long-term incentive and value-sharing mechanism,” said YT Jia, Founder and Global CEO of FF. “By linking the core team’s long-term interests to the growth of our robotics business and enterprise value, we aim to align the interests of our team, the Company and our stockholders. We believe this will encourage a partnership mindset, sustained commitment and long-term value creation.” FF aims to build the world’s only “One-Brain Multi-Form Multi-Capability” FF EAI Robot World. Its “Four-Core Full-Stack AI” ecosystem is taking shape, and Robot World 2.0 is complete. Spanning three robot forms, five series, 11 models and 24 products, FF believes its lineup offers the most complete range of robot forms, broadest size coverage and most models of any U.S. robotics company—providing industries and users with an EAI Brain, solutions and data across those forms. At its 919 FF EAI Robotics “Four-Core Full-Stack AI” Ecosystem New Product Series Launch, FF launched nine EAI Device configurations across two robot forms, three series and five models: FF All-New Futurist, FF Master Mini, FX Aegis Hyper, FX Aegis Mega and FX Aegis Classic Ultra-W. All nine are now available for sale and delivery. FF also launched four Industry Productivity Solutions for K-12 Education, Research, Security and Inspection. By linking the core team’s incentives to the growth of the robotics business, FF aims to strengthen operating efficiency and value creation while keeping stockholder interests at the forefront. Second, for the Company, the plan is expected to strengthen its ability to attract and retain top talent, encourage an entrepreneurial and partnership-oriented culture, and build the team needed to compete in the robotics industry. Finally, for the industry, FF EAI Robotics aims to become the first robotics company to implement a partnership model, offering an example of how long-term talent incentives can strengthen organizational capabilities across the robotics sector. passages: A Saudi engineer at artificial intelligence giant OpenAI was arrested and charged with attempting to bug confidential meetings by planting secret recording devices in executive conference rooms, federal prosecutors said.

OpenAI discovered a “surreptitious audio recording device” stuffed into a USB port on the back of a TV in a conference room — wrapped in toilet paper in an attempt to conceal the device, according to the complaint.

Meetings in that conference room apparently involved high-level discussions of the company’s confidential plans, such as proprietary research, OpenAI’s technical capabilities, its government relationships and more.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who is from Saudi Arabia, is in federal custody after his arrest Friday.
An OpenAI spokesperson told the California Post that there was no indications of Alfozan inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code or customer data.
Alfozan also used chatbots to plot the alleged recording efforts, asking about OpenAI’s building addresses, meeting room capacities and calendars, authorities said.

sources.title: Saudi OpenAI engineer bugged top secret meetings with toilet paper trickery, feds say after bombshell arrest - New York Post
passages: A Saudi engineer at artificial intelligence giant OpenAI was arrested and charged with attempting to bug confidential meetings by planting secret recording devices in executive conference rooms, federal prosecutors said.

OpenAI discovered a “surreptitious audio recording device” stuffed into a USB port on the back of a TV in a conference room — wrapped in toilet paper in an attempt to conceal the device, according to the complaint.

Meetings in that conference room apparently involved high-level discussions of the company’s confidential plans, such as proprietary research, OpenAI’s technical capabilities, its government relationships and more.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who is from Saudi Arabia, is in federal custody after his arrest Friday.
An OpenAI spokesperson told the California Post that there was no indications of Alfozan inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code or customer data.
Alfozan also used chatbots to plot the alleged recording efforts, asking about OpenAI’s building addresses, meeting room capacities and calendars, authorities said.

extraction.body: Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s startup Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the CEO’s secretive robotics project. Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company’s ultimately unsuccessful Project Titan effort to make an autonomous electric car. He had a previous stint at Apple as VP of Mac hardware engineering, but he left the company in 2013 to become Tesla’s chief vehicle engineer, where he helped oversee the Model 3 sedan. In 2021, Field was hired by Ford to run the automaker’s electric vehicle and software division, a position he held until earlier this year. Mind Robotics said Field will oversee its effort to build “universally capable robots” for the purpose of working in Rivian’s factories, as well as other applications. The startup was founded by Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe in 2025, and has since raised over $1 billion in financing. extraction.body: In a big coup for Mind Robotics, the industrial robotics startup spun out of Rivian ( RIVN ) announced it has hired former Ford ( F ) EV chief Doug Field as its president. Ford announced Field's exit six months ago, and now Mind Robotics gets one of the auto industry's most experienced hardware engineers, who also cut his teeth at Tesla. The hire comes as Mind attempts to harness AI trained on Rivian's factory floor into robots it can sell to the wider manufacturing world. Field will oversee product, engineering, and operations and will work alongside Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe, who founded Mind and chairs its board, according to a press release on Tuesday. Mind didn't disclose his pay or start date. "Doug is a remarkable leader with a track record of delivering new technologies in successful products," Scaringe said in a statement. "He has an incredible ability to foster great teams that take on big, complex ideas." Field's resume reads like a who's who of the biggest tech companies. He led Mac hardware engineering at Apple ( AAPL ), then ran engineering at Tesla ( TSLA ) as senior vice president and oversaw development of the Model 3. He later went back to Apple to lead its Special Projects Group, widely reported to be home to the company's secretive car effort, before rejoining Ford in 2021. At Ford, Field rose to chief EV, digital and design officer, reporting to CEO Jim Farley. He was behind the skunkworks team that built the automaker's low-cost Universal EV platform . His exit came in a broader leadership shake-up that folded his team into a new product creation and industrialization organization under COO Kumar Galhotra. "Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important - and difficult - engineering challenges of our time," Field said in the statement. "I'm thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America." Mind Robotics was founded last year and was first disclosed to Rivian in November. The startup is building AI foundation models, robots, and deployment infrastructure for industrial automation. Rivian is its first customer and launch partner, giving Mind a high-volume factory where it can train and deploy its robots. Rivian also kept a minority stake in the company. Mind has raised more than $1 billion, including a $500 million Series A co-led by Accel and Andreessen Horowitz in March, and a $400 million round led by Kleiner Perkins in May, which valued the company at more than $3 billion, per the Wall Street Journal . Scaringe has argued that humanoid robots are needlessly complex for most factory work. Investors will be watching to see whether new hire Doug Field, the engineer who helped bring the Model 3 to market, can do the same for robots on the factory floor. extraction.body: Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s startup Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the CEO’s secretive robotics project. Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company’s ultimately unsuccessful Project Titan effort to make an autonomous electric car. He had a previous stint at Apple as VP of Mac hardware engineering, but he left the company in 2013 to become Tesla’s chief vehicle engineer, where he helped oversee the Model 3 sedan. In 2021, Field was hired by Ford to run the automaker’s electric vehicle and software division, a position he held until earlier this year. Mind Robotics said Field will oversee its effort to build “universally capable robots” for the purpose of working in Rivian’s factories, as well as other applications. The startup was founded by Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe in 2025, and has since raised over $1 billion in financing. While the company has yet to show off any of its robots in public, the startup says its robots are being designed with “dexterity and physical reasoning” that’s required for industrial work. “Doug is a remarkable leader with a track record of delivering new technologies in successful products, and I couldn’t be more excited to be building Mind with him,” Scaringe said in a statement. That’s exactly what Mind needs as we deploy robots into real factories and beyond.” Field joins Mind Robotics at a major turning point for the field of robotics, with rapid advances in physical AI colliding with major hurdles in hardware and software development. Several companies, like Tesla and Hyundai, are pursuing humanoid robots for factory and warehouse work — even as experts note that making a robot act like a human is easier than scaling the technology for practical work. Mind Robotics hasn’t confirmed whether it’s working on a humanoid design or something else entirely. The company has been on a hiring spree and currently has 32 open positions. Scaringe, who serves as acting CEO and chair of Mind Robotics, has said he wants to keep the companies separate, rather than try to combine the work like Tesla. That said, the companies are certainly linked in several ways. Mind Robotics is using AI training data from Rivian, and the robots will be initially tested in Rivian’s factories. Rivian also owns equity in Mind Robotics and will be the first customer for its robots. Field said he is excited for the challenge in running the new startup. “Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important—and difficult—engineering challenges of our time,” he said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. The next governor will undoubtedly reckon with the construction boom in the Badger State of the increasingly controversial factories of artificial intelligence.

As more massive technology centers are stood up across the state, Wisconsin voters of all political stripes are growing more opposed to them, with nearly 80% of voters saying in a recent statewide poll that the costs of building data centers outweigh the benefits.
“There should be full transparency, and we will ban NDAs that keep communities in the dark,” Tiffany told the Journal Sentinel.

Both candidates also said they want the companies that build the data centers to pay for their own energy. “Any costs created by data centers must be paid by the facilities themselves, not passed on to Wisconsin families and businesses through higher utility bills, and they must adhere to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge and bring their own energy,” Tiffany said, referring to an order issued by President Donald Trump on data center regulation.

extraction.body: MADISON – The two major candidates running to be Wisconsin’s next governor are battling to gain the upper hand on an emerging issue that neither political party owns yet: data centers. The next governor will undoubtedly reckon with the construction boom in the Badger State of the increasingly controversial factories of artificial intelligence. As more massive technology centers are stood up across the state, Wisconsin voters of all political stripes are growing more opposed to them, with nearly 80% of voters saying in a recent statewide poll that the costs of building data centers outweigh the benefits. Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany are each seeking to portray the other as friendlier to big tech, with Tiffany placing seven figures worth of ads across the state dubbing his opponent as “Data Center David Crowley,” and Crowley pointing to Tiffany’s voting record on federal legislation that sought to make it easier to build projects like data centers. Former Democratic candidate Francesca Hong built a formidable following during the primary race, in part, because she called for a moratorium on construction of new data centers in the state ? the only candidate to do so. Crowley and Tiffany are opposed to statewide moratoriums but are calling for stricter regulations governing how such developments may move forward. The starkest contrast between the two is related to the giant carrot state governments can offer data center builders: tax subsidies. Tiffany is calling to end tax incentives outright while Crowley said he would make it harder to get them. Both agree on banning non-disclosure agreements, disagree on subsidies Both Crowley and Tiffany said they would not seek to override the right of local communities to reject developments if they don’t want them. And both said they would seek to ban developers’ use of non-disclosure agreements that keep project details from the public. “These data centers are being built by big tech and we know how these companies try to use our data and hide their motives,” Crowley said in response to a series of questions from the Journal Sentinel about each candidate’s positions on data centers. “If they are building to benefit our communities then they should have nothing to hide. extraction.body: Gorman, who has been on the Rock County Board of Supervisors since 2024, began organizing with citizens across the county who feared that the project would raise utility bills, diminish air quality, and drain the county’s groundwater, joining a growing nationwide backlash against data centers. “I’ve never seen engagement like this on any normal development issue,” Gorman said. “People don’t like that they didn’t have a vote on whether social media could take over our society. And now people see A.I. getting ready to take things over and potentially upset lives, upset society, upset jobs, and they want the ability to have a say in that.” Local residents helped set up informal community meetings to discuss the data center at the public library, and opposition kept building. “I won very conservative parts of the town of Beloit that I had previously lost, purely on the data-center issue,” he told me. “You can knock seven doors and hear seven different reasons why people don’t want this.” A recent Gallup poll found that more than seventy per cent of Americans oppose data centers in their area. And, during the past several weeks, data centers have become increasingly toxic in midterm elections across the country. Opposition has become particularly central to contests in Rust Belt states, such as Republican-trending Ohio, where anti-data-center policies have appeared to boost the campaigns of the Democrats Amy Acton, who is running for governor, and Sherrod Brown, who is running for Senate. Brown’s opponent is the incumbent Jon Husted, who previously, as lieutenant governor, helped usher in an explosion of data centers in the state, many of which were developed after Ohio offered them lucrative tax breaks. Brown’s ability to hammer Husted on this issue is alarming Republican operatives, who see a Husted victory as crucial to holding a majority in the Senate. This month, Axios released a private memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee warning that data centers have become an “anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.” Other politicians are distancing themselves from their previous positions, including Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, who is up for reëlection in November, and used to champion data centers. Last week, he signed an executive order that he claimed “enacted the strictest requirements IN THE NATION” for data-center permits. “We will not be bulldozed by the lawyers for these big tech companies.” But nowhere have the politics of data centers been more strained than in the Wisconsin governor’s race. Earlier this month, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley narrowly won the Democratic nomination after one of the most chaotic and unusual primaries in the state’s history. The front-runner through most of the primary had been Francesca Hong, a democratic-socialist assemblywoman from Madison whose success was partially driven by her vociferous opposition to data centers; her signature policy proposal during the campaign was a one-year moratorium on new data centers, which none of her opponents supported. (In July, Governor Kathy Hochul made New York the first state to enact such a policy.) Hong also called for cutting state funding and tax breaks for companies that lay off workers as a result of adopting A.I. She lost to Crowley by fewer than four thousand votes after attacks from a hostile Democratic establishment; a disastrous appearance on CNN in which she did not walk back a 2020 tweet calling to “cancel Thanksgiving”; and a stream of late money into Crowley’s campaign, including from building-trades unions, who support data centers because of the jobs that they’ll create for their members. Shortly after he beat Hong, Crowley was asked what the biggest difference between them was. He answered, “data centers,” then went on to explain that, while he’s for “guardrails” on them, he is against Hong’s moratorium, because it doesn’t address existing data centers. It was a curious issue for Crowley to single out, especially if he was hoping to attract Hong voters. And, while most politicians who have opposed data centers have been Democrats, Crowley’s Republican opponent, Representative Tom Tiffany, saw a populist opening and pounced. He posted an edited clip of the interview, and the issue soon became the centerpiece of his campaign. (It is the only specific policy currently detailed on his website.) He dubbed Crowley “Data Center David,” and ran ads with a clip from a primary forum in which Crowley said, “There’s an opportunity for us to really become an A.I. and a data hub not only for the entire country but for the entire globe.” In the years since the exemptions went into effect, Wisconsin has become a major hub of data-center construction. More than forty-six billion dollars’ worth of data-center-development projects are currently under construction or being considered in the state, according to an estimate by the nonprofit newsroom Wisconsin Watch. Recently, a Seattle-based company called Cloverleaf Infrastructure has been drawing national attention as “A.I. prospectors” in Wisconsin—securing large plots of land from farmers and other landowners for tech companies. Its biggest success so far is facilitating the development of Oracle and OpenAI’s fifteen-billion-dollar data-center campus in Port Washington, a small town in southeastern Wisconsin. Hyper-scale data centers often demand new natural-gas power plants and transmission lines, and Wisconsin’s Public Service Commission approves or denies permits for such developments, with no requirement for input from local communities. Recently, the commission predicted that the state’s power-generation needs will rise by forty per cent in the next six years, largely because of data centers. Seventy-eight per cent of Wisconsin’s residents now oppose data centers, according to an August poll from Marquette University Law School, up from fifty-five per cent this past October. “Republicans have become more opposed, but Democrats have become even more opposed,” Charles Franklin, the poll’s director, told me. The Marquette poll also showed similar levels of opposition across the state, even in places where there is no proposed development. There are no plans for data centers in the assembly district of Ben Gruber, a Democratic assembly candidate in southwestern Wisconsin, but he has found that the issue still resonates with voters. “Data centers are a physical target of an emotional, visceral populist anger,” Gruber told me. “What everybody is most upset about is the corporate welfare, while our communities suffer,” he said. Since Tiffany’s attacks began, Crowley has moved in Hong’s general direction, emphasizing his requirements—using exclusively renewable energy to power new data centers, building them with union labor—for developers to receive the tax breaks. But he has stopped short of calling for repealing those exemptions, giving Tiffany an opening to try and gain a populist edge on the issue. Last week, Tiffany, who grew up on a dairy farm, embarked on a tour called “Protecting Wisconsin Farmland,” continuing to cultivate his image as a folksy, rural Wisconsinite devoted to beloved institutions like the family farm and the tavern. (One treacly campaign sign reads “You Betcha! Tom Tiffany for Governor.”) His data-center-focussed attack ads emphasize that message.

extraction.body: In a governor’s race that has focused more on data center construction than artificial intelligence technology, Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Tuesday announced a plan for state regulations on AI aimed at protecting vulnerable Wisconsinites. In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms. Some key components of the plan include: Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, is running for governor against Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany in what polling from Marquette University Law School shows could be another close governor’s race in Wisconsin. AI policy debates between the two candidates in the months since the August primary have mostly been focused on the planning and construction of AI data centers, rather than the technology itself. In a statement, Tiffany also said Wisconsin needs “commonsense guardrails” to protect children and older adults, including holding companies accountable for platforms that allow creation of sexually explicit images or engage minors in inappropriate chatbot conversations. Tiffany said he also wants to prevent personal data from “falling into the hands of foreign adversaries, including Communist China.” “As governor, I will also support commonsense age-verification requirements for app providers, strengthen parental-consent protections, and give parents greater control over their children’s online activity,” Tiffany said. Crowley’s proposed state-level AI regulations land as President Donald Trump has dismissed calls for guardrails and warnings from technology company leaders asking for government oversight as their platforms become more advanced. Trump in May 2025 signed the Take it Down Act, which criminalized the online publication of real and AI-generated intimate images and requires social media platforms to remove them once notified of their existence. Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025. Other proposed federal legislation has not advanced, including bills requiring public reporting of safety incidents by AI companies and requiring labels on any AI-generated content. Crowley in a statement said he would not “wait around for DC to act” on additional AI regulations if he is elected. “Like so many parents, Ericka and I are raising our three girls in the age of social media and AI, and we’re navigating things no generation before us has ever had to, worrying about whether a stranger is messaging our kids, or a fake picture of our daughter is going around school, or even scammers trying to drain a grandparent’s life savings,” Crowley said. The proposals in Crowley’s regulatory plan would require state legislative action. They echo recent bipartisan efforts signed into law by Gov. Tony Evers, including a series of bills that classified sextortion as a crime and provided additional recourse for victims and their families. Additionally, Attorney General Josh Kaul in August announced Wisconsin could receive up to $313 million in a settlement social media company Meta made with 47 states in a case that alleged addictive components of its platforms threatened teens’ mental health. coreStoryFacts.text: MADISON – The two major candidates running to be Wisconsin’s next governor are battling to gain the upper hand on an emerging issue that neither political party owns yet: data centers.
The next governor will undoubtedly reckon with the construction boom in the Badger State of the increasingly controversial factories of artificial intelligence.

As more massive technology centers are stood up across the state, Wisconsin voters of all political stripes are growing more opposed to them, with nearly 80% of voters saying in a recent statewide poll that the costs of building data centers outweigh the benefits.
“There should be full transparency, and we will ban NDAs that keep communities in the dark,” Tiffany told the Journal Sentinel.

Both candidates also said they want the companies that build the data centers to pay for their own energy. “Any costs created by data centers must be paid by the facilities themselves, not passed on to Wisconsin families and businesses through higher utility bills, and they must adhere to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge and bring their own energy,” Tiffany said, referring to an order issued by President Donald Trump on data center regulation.

Tiffany is calling to end tax incentives outright while Crowley said he would make it harder to get them.

Crowley and Tiffany are opposed to statewide moratoriums but are calling for stricter regulations governing how such developments may move forward.

extraction.body: MADISON – The two major candidates running to be Wisconsin’s next governor are battling to gain the upper hand on an emerging issue that neither political party owns yet: data centers. The next governor will undoubtedly reckon with the construction boom in the Badger State of the increasingly controversial factories of artificial intelligence. As more massive technology centers are stood up across the state, Wisconsin voters of all political stripes are growing more opposed to them, with nearly 80% of voters saying in a recent statewide poll that the costs of building data centers outweigh the benefits. Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany are each seeking to portray the other as friendlier to big tech, with Tiffany placing seven figures worth of ads across the state dubbing his opponent as “Data Center David Crowley,” and Crowley pointing to Tiffany’s voting record on federal legislation that sought to make it easier to build projects like data centers. Former Democratic candidate Francesca Hong built a formidable following during the primary race, in part, because she called for a moratorium on construction of new data centers in the state ? the only candidate to do so. Crowley and Tiffany are opposed to statewide moratoriums but are calling for stricter regulations governing how such developments may move forward. The starkest contrast between the two is related to the giant carrot state governments can offer data center builders: tax subsidies. Tiffany is calling to end tax incentives outright while Crowley said he would make it harder to get them. Both agree on banning non-disclosure agreements, disagree on subsidies Both Crowley and Tiffany said they would not seek to override the right of local communities to reject developments if they don’t want them. And both said they would seek to ban developers’ use of non-disclosure agreements that keep project details from the public. “These data centers are being built by big tech and we know how these companies try to use our data and hide their motives,” Crowley said in response to a series of questions from the Journal Sentinel about each candidate’s positions on data centers. “If they are building to benefit our communities then they should have nothing to hide. Everything they do should be done so with oversight and public transparency.” “There should be full transparency, and we will ban NDAs that keep communities in the dark,” Tiffany told the Journal Sentinel. Both candidates also said they want the companies that build the data centers to pay for their own energy. “Any costs created by data centers must be paid by the facilities themselves, not passed on to Wisconsin families and businesses through higher utility bills, and they must adhere to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge and bring their own energy,” Tiffany said, referring to an order issued by President Donald Trump on data center regulation. extraction.body: Gorman, who has been on the Rock County Board of Supervisors since 2024, began organizing with citizens across the county who feared that the project would raise utility bills, diminish air quality, and drain the county’s groundwater, joining a growing nationwide backlash against data centers. “I’ve never seen engagement like this on any normal development issue,” Gorman said. “People don’t like that they didn’t have a vote on whether social media could take over our society. And now people see A.I. getting ready to take things over and potentially upset lives, upset society, upset jobs, and they want the ability to have a say in that.” Local residents helped set up informal community meetings to discuss the data center at the public library, and opposition kept building. “I won very conservative parts of the town of Beloit that I had previously lost, purely on the data-center issue,” he told me. “You can knock seven doors and hear seven different reasons why people don’t want this.” A recent Gallup poll found that more than seventy per cent of Americans oppose data centers in their area. And, during the past several weeks, data centers have become increasingly toxic in midterm elections across the country. Opposition has become particularly central to contests in Rust Belt states, such as Republican-trending Ohio, where anti-data-center policies have appeared to boost the campaigns of the Democrats Amy Acton, who is running for governor, and Sherrod Brown, who is running for Senate. Brown’s opponent is the incumbent Jon Husted, who previously, as lieutenant governor, helped usher in an explosion of data centers in the state, many of which were developed after Ohio offered them lucrative tax breaks. Brown’s ability to hammer Husted on this issue is alarming Republican operatives, who see a Husted victory as crucial to holding a majority in the Senate. This month, Axios released a private memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee warning that data centers have become an “anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.” Other politicians are distancing themselves from their previous positions, including Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, who is up for reëlection in November, and used to champion data centers. Last week, he signed an executive order that he claimed “enacted the strictest requirements IN THE NATION” for data-center permits. “We will not be bulldozed by the lawyers for these big tech companies.” But nowhere have the politics of data centers been more strained than in the Wisconsin governor’s race. Earlier this month, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley narrowly won the Democratic nomination after one of the most chaotic and unusual primaries in the state’s history. The front-runner through most of the primary had been Francesca Hong, a democratic-socialist assemblywoman from Madison whose success was partially driven by her vociferous opposition to data centers; her signature policy proposal during the campaign was a one-year moratorium on new data centers, which none of her opponents supported. (In July, Governor Kathy Hochul made New York the first state to enact such a policy.) Hong also called for cutting state funding and tax breaks for companies that lay off workers as a result of adopting A.I. She lost to Crowley by fewer than four thousand votes after attacks from a hostile Democratic establishment; a disastrous appearance on CNN in which she did not walk back a 2020 tweet calling to “cancel Thanksgiving”; and a stream of late money into Crowley’s campaign, including from building-trades unions, who support data centers because of the jobs that they’ll create for their members. Shortly after he beat Hong, Crowley was asked what the biggest difference between them was. He answered, “data centers,” then went on to explain that, while he’s for “guardrails” on them, he is against Hong’s moratorium, because it doesn’t address existing data centers. It was a curious issue for Crowley to single out, especially if he was hoping to attract Hong voters. And, while most politicians who have opposed data centers have been Democrats, Crowley’s Republican opponent, Representative Tom Tiffany, saw a populist opening and pounced. He posted an edited clip of the interview, and the issue soon became the centerpiece of his campaign. (It is the only specific policy currently detailed on his website.) He dubbed Crowley “Data Center David,” and ran ads with a clip from a primary forum in which Crowley said, “There’s an opportunity for us to really become an A.I. and a data hub not only for the entire country but for the entire globe.” In the years since the exemptions went into effect, Wisconsin has become a major hub of data-center construction. More than forty-six billion dollars’ worth of data-center-development projects are currently under construction or being considered in the state, according to an estimate by the nonprofit newsroom Wisconsin Watch. Recently, a Seattle-based company called Cloverleaf Infrastructure has been drawing national attention as “A.I. prospectors” in Wisconsin—securing large plots of land from farmers and other landowners for tech companies. Its biggest success so far is facilitating the development of Oracle and OpenAI’s fifteen-billion-dollar data-center campus in Port Washington, a small town in southeastern Wisconsin. Hyper-scale data centers often demand new natural-gas power plants and transmission lines, and Wisconsin’s Public Service Commission approves or denies permits for such developments, with no requirement for input from local communities. Recently, the commission predicted that the state’s power-generation needs will rise by forty per cent in the next six years, largely because of data centers. Seventy-eight per cent of Wisconsin’s residents now oppose data centers, according to an August poll from Marquette University Law School, up from fifty-five per cent this past October. “Republicans have become more opposed, but Democrats have become even more opposed,” Charles Franklin, the poll’s director, told me. The Marquette poll also showed similar levels of opposition across the state, even in places where there is no proposed development. There are no plans for data centers in the assembly district of Ben Gruber, a Democratic assembly candidate in southwestern Wisconsin, but he has found that the issue still resonates with voters. “Data centers are a physical target of an emotional, visceral populist anger,” Gruber told me. “What everybody is most upset about is the corporate welfare, while our communities suffer,” he said. Since Tiffany’s attacks began, Crowley has moved in Hong’s general direction, emphasizing his requirements—using exclusively renewable energy to power new data centers, building them with union labor—for developers to receive the tax breaks. But he has stopped short of calling for repealing those exemptions, giving Tiffany an opening to try and gain a populist edge on the issue. Last week, Tiffany, who grew up on a dairy farm, embarked on a tour called “Protecting Wisconsin Farmland,” continuing to cultivate his image as a folksy, rural Wisconsinite devoted to beloved institutions like the family farm and the tavern. (One treacly campaign sign reads “You Betcha! Tom Tiffany for Governor.”) His data-center-focussed attack ads emphasize that message.

passages: In a governor’s race that has focused more on data center construction than artificial intelligence technology, Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Tuesday announced a plan for state regulations on AI aimed at protecting vulnerable Wisconsinites.
In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms.
Brittany Carloni joined Wisconsin Watch as the state government and politics reporter in September 2025.
She returned home to Wisconsin after more than eight years away from the Badger State.
Brittany is originally from the Milwaukee area and holds a bachelor’s degree in journalism from Marquette University.

extraction.body: In a governor’s race that has focused more on data center construction than artificial intelligence technology, Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Tuesday announced a plan for state regulations on AI aimed at protecting vulnerable Wisconsinites. In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms. Some key components of the plan include: Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, is running for governor against Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany in what polling from Marquette University Law School shows could be another close governor’s race in Wisconsin. AI policy debates between the two candidates in the months since the August primary have mostly been focused on the planning and construction of AI data centers, rather than the technology itself. In a statement, Tiffany also said Wisconsin needs “commonsense guardrails” to protect children and older adults, including holding companies accountable for platforms that allow creation of sexually explicit images or engage minors in inappropriate chatbot conversations. Tiffany said he also wants to prevent personal data from “falling into the hands of foreign adversaries, including Communist China.” “As governor, I will also support commonsense age-verification requirements for app providers, strengthen parental-consent protections, and give parents greater control over their children’s online activity,” Tiffany said. Crowley’s proposed state-level AI regulations land as President Donald Trump has dismissed calls for guardrails and warnings from technology company leaders asking for government oversight as their platforms become more advanced. Trump in May 2025 signed the Take it Down Act, which criminalized the online publication of real and AI-generated intimate images and requires social media platforms to remove them once notified of their existence. Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025. Other proposed federal legislation has not advanced, including bills requiring public reporting of safety incidents by AI companies and requiring labels on any AI-generated content. Crowley in a statement said he would not “wait around for DC to act” on additional AI regulations if he is elected. “Like so many parents, Ericka and I are raising our three girls in the age of social media and AI, and we’re navigating things no generation before us has ever had to, worrying about whether a stranger is messaging our kids, or a fake picture of our daughter is going around school, or even scammers trying to drain a grandparent’s life savings,” Crowley said. The proposals in Crowley’s regulatory plan would require state legislative action. They echo recent bipartisan efforts signed into law by Gov. Tony Evers, including a series of bills that classified sextortion as a crime and provided additional recourse for victims and their families. Additionally, Attorney General Josh Kaul in August announced Wisconsin could receive up to $313 million in a settlement social media company Meta made with 47 states in a case that alleged addictive components of its platforms threatened teens’ mental health. Tiffany said he also wants to prevent personal data from “falling into the hands of foreign adversaries, including Communist China.”

sources.title: Apple releases HomeView smart home hub with screen as showcase for Siri AI - CNBC
passages: Apple said its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.
Apple on Tuesday announced a home hub called HomeView, marking CEO John Ternus' first launch outside of iPhones since he took over from Tim Cook at the start of September.
Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad.

"It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's marketing head Greg Joswiak said in a statement.
The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch.

The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month.
Apple is emphasizing privacy, and said on Tuesday that its Apple Home Collection accessories encrypt data so that only the user and people they share with can see it.
Other smart home cameras, for example, maintain limited access to user video, or store it on servers.
Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence.
People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone.

"Apple always waits for an ecosystem to develop first until they are positive they can provide a stellar user experience," said Jennifer Kent, principal analyst at Parks Associates, which conducts research on the connected home.
Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday.
Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price.
Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories.
But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage.
It also comes as Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster.

extraction.body: Apple on Tuesday announced a home hub called HomeView, marking CEO John Ternus' first launch outside of iPhones since he took over from Tim Cook at the start of September. Apple said the device with a 7-inch screen was designed to be mounted on a wall or placed on a table. It's designed for multiple people in a household, and will recognize the user by their face to display pertinent information. It starts at $299 and ships on Nov. 13. Tuesday's launch event is the second under Ternus, who was the company's longtime hardware boss before being promoted to CEO. Last month, Apple announced new models of its most important product, the iPhone, including a foldable model called the Duo that retails for nearly $2,000. Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday. The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and has a redesigned remote that can play a sound if it is lost. Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price. The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month. Apple said HomeView features Siri AI, which can answer a broad range of questions. Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad. It has a built-in speaker for playing music. "It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's marketing head Greg Joswiak said in a statement. Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence. It can also be used to make FaceTime calls and as a digital photo frame. It's equipped with an Apple A18 chip. It supports up to six users. Apple TV, HomePods, and HomeView are included in Apple's Wearables, Home, and Accessories category, which reported $7.88 billion in sales in the most recent quarter ended June, which was about 7% of the company's total revenue. The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch. But while Apple has dabbled in home products and platforms in the past, Tuesday's announcement shows Apple is making its home products a higher priority under Ternus. "Apple always waits for an ecosystem to develop first until they are positive they can provide a stellar user experience," said Jennifer Kent, principal analyst at Parks Associates, which conducts research on the connected home. Apple said its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple is emphasizing privacy, and said on Tuesday that its Apple Home Collection accessories encrypt data so that only the user and people they share with can see it. Other smart home cameras, for example, maintain limited access to user video, or store it on servers. "They are going above and beyond what a lot of other companies do when it comes to privacy and security protections," Kent said. Apple's integration with the smart home is not just about sales, but also helps further lock customers into its ecosystem. People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone. HomeView can also become a smart home dashboard, Apple said. It can be used to view camera feeds, adjust the thermostat, or lock connected doors around the house. Apple said that setting up a new smart home device takes one tap from the user's iPhone. Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories. But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage. It also comes as Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster. Apple's new Apple TV 4K got a price hike from $199 to $299, and follows a similar price increase earlier this year, after Cook said that memory costs for Apple were unsustainable. It can also be used to make FaceTime calls and as a digital photo frame. It's equipped with an Apple A18 chip. It supports up to six users.

Apple TV, HomePods, and HomeView are included in Apple's Wearables, Home, and Accessories category, which reported $7.88 billion in sales in the most recent quarter ended June, which was about 7% of the company's total revenue. The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch.
But while Apple has dabbled in home products and platforms in the past, Tuesday's announcement shows Apple is making its home products a higher priority under Ternus.

"Apple always waits for an ecosystem to develop first until they are positive they can provide a stellar user experience," said Jennifer Kent, principal analyst at Parks Associates, which conducts research on the connected home.

Apple said its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.

Apple is emphasizing privacy, and said on Tuesday that its Apple Home Collection accessories encrypt data so that only the user and people they share with can see it. Other smart home cameras, for example, maintain limited access to user video, or store it on servers.
"They are going above and beyond what a lot of other companies do when it comes to privacy and security protections," Kent said.

Apple's integration with the smart home is not just about sales, but also helps further lock customers into its ecosystem. People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone.
HomeView can also become a smart home dashboard, Apple said. It can be used to view camera feeds, adjust the thermostat, or lock connected doors around the house.
Apple said that setting up a new smart home device takes one tap from the user's iPhone.

Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories. But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage. It also comes as Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster.
Apple's new Apple TV 4K got a price hike from $199 to $299, and follows a similar price increase earlier this year, after Cook said that memory costs for Apple were unsustainable.

extraction.body: Apple on Tuesday announced a home hub called HomeView, marking CEO John Ternus' first launch outside of iPhones since he took over from Tim Cook at the start of September. Apple said the device with a 7-inch screen was designed to be mounted on a wall or placed on a table. It's designed for multiple people in a household, and will recognize the user by their face to display pertinent information. It starts at $299 and ships on Nov. 13. Tuesday's launch event is the second under Ternus, who was the company's longtime hardware boss before being promoted to CEO. Last month, Apple announced new models of its most important product, the iPhone, including a foldable model called the Duo that retails for nearly $2,000. Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday. The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and has a redesigned remote that can play a sound if it is lost. Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price. The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month. Apple said HomeView features Siri AI, which can answer a broad range of questions. Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad. It has a built-in speaker for playing music. "It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's marketing head Greg Joswiak said in a statement. Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence. It can also be used to make FaceTime calls and as a digital photo frame. It's equipped with an Apple A18 chip. It supports up to six users. Apple TV, HomePods, and HomeView are included in Apple's Wearables, Home, and Accessories category, which reported $7.88 billion in sales in the most recent quarter ended June, which was about 7% of the company's total revenue. The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch. sources.title: Intel to keep working on Elon Musk's Terafab chip venture - Yahoo Finance
passages: According to Bloomberg , Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan has indicated that the chipmaker plans to remain a partner in Terafab, Elon Musk's planned chip manufacturing complex in Texas.
Tan spoke to reporters on Wednesday before appearing at a Tokyo ceremony celebrating half a century of Intel's presence in Japan.
Terafab is a joint venture between SpaceX and Tesla to manufacture chips at a site in Grimes County, Texas.

When Intel first announced its involvement in the project in April, Intel said at the time that its expertise spanning chip design, fabrication, and advanced packaging would help the venture hit its target of generating one terawatt of annual computing capacity for AI and robotics applications.
Tesla and SpaceX launched the project with an initial investment of $16.8 billion and a planned workforce of at least 3,000 people.
Chips produced there are intended for use in Tesla's Optimus robots and Cybercabs, as well as space-based data centers that SpaceX is developing.
Total spending across all phases of the project could reach as much as $119 billion .
SpaceX has proposed spending $55 billion to begin construction of the facility, according to a public notice posted on Grimes County's website.
During Tesla's most recent quarterly earnings call, Musk indicated that Intel's 14A process would serve as the manufacturing backbone for chip production at Terafab.
Also on Wednesday, Musk sought to clarify the scope of any TSMC involvement.
"We will build and run the fab," Musk wrote in a post responding to a Tesla commentator.
Intel stock rose 2.18% in Wednesday premarket trading to $114.95.

sources.title: Intel stock drops after Elon Musk hints Terafab could partner with a rival chipmaker - AOL.com
passages: Why : The stock dropped as the week began following a weekend post from Elon Musk that hinted at a deepening partnership with an Intel rival.

On Saturday, Musk addressed a report from tech journalist and researcher Tim Culpan, who claimed that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company could work with Terafab, Musk's planned semiconductor plant being developed by Tesla , SpaceX, and Intel.

What it means : There's no deal yet between Musk's companies and TSMC, but the market's reaction to the possibility of a partnership has spooked investors who may have been betting on Intel being the top hardware beneficiary of the Terafab project.
Data from Stocktwits shows that sentiment among retail investors shifted to bearish following Musk's post.
Shares of the US chipmaker are up 213% year to date.
Intel stock fell dropped 3 %to start the week.

extraction.body: Elon Musk has his eyes set on something that even the world's largest technology companies have struggled to accomplish: Manufacture advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips at an unprecedented scale. Surprisingly, Intel ( INTC +1.44% ) could emerge as one of the biggest beneficiaries of this vision. Musk's Terafab project brings together Tesla ( TSLA -0.74% ) and Space Exploration Technologies ( SPCX -4.21% ) in an effort to reduce outside dependence on semiconductor manufacturing. For a company trying to turn around its foundry leadership, investors may be underestimating how this could transform Intel in the AI infrastructure era. Terafab is a proposed semiconductor manufacturing facility in Grimes County, Texas. So far, Tesla and SpaceX have committed initial investments of $16.8 billion for the first phase of the project. Terfab's goal is to stitch together chip design, advanced logic and memory manufacturing, and semiconductor packaging within a vertically integrated operation. Musk's long-term goal is to produce enough annual chip production to support 1 terawatt of computing power. Terafab aims to produce two categories of processors. The first will power Tesla's autonomous vehicles , Optimus humanoid robots, and other AI applications operating here on Earth. The second is meant to support SpaceX's plans for space-based data centers . In April, Intel's participation in Terafab was confirmed, positioning its manufacturing expertise and advanced semiconductor technologies alongside Musk's grand plans. The company has been developing its 18A and 14A manufacturing processes , which are central to its effort to compete with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing 's leading foundry capabilities. Intel's foundry business stands to benefit enormously from securing a high-profile customer with substantial long-term chip requirements. More importantly, there is already some encouraging evidence of improving execution. During the second quarter, Intel Foundry generated $5.8 billion in revenue, although most of that came from manufacturing chips for Intel's own products. External foundry revenue was only $293 million, and the division reported an operating loss of approximately $2.1 billion as a whole. This is why Terafab matters so much. If Intel can prove that its technology meets Musk's requirements, it could strengthen credibility with other AI chip designers. Given the nascent nature of the project, Intel's potential manufacturing volumes and financial impact remain highly uncertain. Nevertheless, the company possesses something valuable: an opportunity to demonstrate that its foundry technology belongs in the same conversation alongside other industry leaders. Terafab represents something different for various companies. For Tesla and SpaceX, it could reduce dependence on outside chip suppliers and support AI-driven growth across autonomous driving and robotics. For Nvidia, it introduces another potential source of competition as more companies develop custom silicon. For Intel, the implications could be transformational. Intel does not need to displace Nvidia as the leading AI accelerator designer. Rather, the company is positioned to profit by helping other companies manufacture their chips. This is an attractive position to be in during an era when AI infrastructure spending continues to accelerate. Still, in the long run, Intel will have to improve manufacturing yields, control capital expenditures (capex), attract additional external customers, and eventually turn its foundry operations profitable. Working on Terafab alone won't accomplish these objectives collectively. For now, I see Intel stock as a speculative buy for investors comfortable with execution risk, understanding Terafab's eventual financial contribution remains uncertain. The bigger thesis is that Intel could become an attractive alternative to Taiwan Semi as demand for advanced AI chip manufacturing grows. Adam Spatacco has positions in Nvidia and Tesla. extraction.body: Elon Musk has his eyes set on something that even the world's largest technology companies have struggled to accomplish: Manufacture advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips at an unprecedented scale. Surprisingly, Intel ( INTC +1.44% ) could emerge as one of the biggest beneficiaries of this vision. Musk's Terafab project brings together Tesla ( TSLA -0.74% ) and Space Exploration Technologies ( SPCX -4.21% ) in an effort to reduce outside dependence on semiconductor manufacturing. For a company trying to turn around its foundry leadership, investors may be underestimating how this could transform Intel in the AI infrastructure era. Terafab is a proposed semiconductor manufacturing facility in Grimes County, Texas. So far, Tesla and SpaceX have committed initial investments of $16.8 billion for the first phase of the project. Terfab's goal is to stitch together chip design, advanced logic and memory manufacturing, and semiconductor packaging within a vertically integrated operation. Musk's long-term goal is to produce enough annual chip production to support 1 terawatt of computing power. Terafab aims to produce two categories of processors. The first will power Tesla's autonomous vehicles , Optimus humanoid robots, and other AI applications operating here on Earth. The second is meant to support SpaceX's plans for space-based data centers . In April, Intel's participation in Terafab was confirmed, positioning its manufacturing expertise and advanced semiconductor technologies alongside Musk's grand plans. The company has been developing its 18A and 14A manufacturing processes , which are central to its effort to compete with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing 's leading foundry capabilities. Intel's foundry business stands to benefit enormously from securing a high-profile customer with substantial long-term chip requirements. More importantly, there is already some encouraging evidence of improving execution. During the second quarter, Intel Foundry generated $5.8 billion in revenue, although most of that came from manufacturing chips for Intel's own products. External foundry revenue was only $293 million, and the division reported an operating loss of approximately $2.1 billion as a whole. This is why Terafab matters so much. If Intel can prove that its technology meets Musk's requirements, it could strengthen credibility with other AI chip designers. Given the nascent nature of the project, Intel's potential manufacturing volumes and financial impact remain highly uncertain. Nevertheless, the company possesses something valuable: an opportunity to demonstrate that its foundry technology belongs in the same conversation alongside other industry leaders. Terafab represents something different for various companies. For Tesla and SpaceX, it could reduce dependence on outside chip suppliers and support AI-driven growth across autonomous driving and robotics. For Nvidia, it introduces another potential source of competition as more companies develop custom silicon. For Intel, the implications could be transformational. Intel does not need to displace Nvidia as the leading AI accelerator designer. Rather, the company is positioned to profit by helping other companies manufacture their chips. This is an attractive position to be in during an era when AI infrastructure spending continues to accelerate. extraction.body: A London court has ruled that the UK government’s likelihood of retaining most of the seized bitcoins has increased. The related bitcoins are valued at approximately £3.8 billion ($5 billion), following a report by the Financial Times that the court determined thousands of Chinese fraud victims cannot claim these coins under UK law. This case involves 61,000 bitcoins seized by the London Metropolitan Police during their investigation of Zhimin Qian, who has admitted to defrauding thousands of people in China. Qian operated a large-scale Ponzi scheme through her company, Tianjin Lantian Gerui Electronic Technology, defrauding over 128,000 investors between 2014 and 2017. She then converted billions of dollars in stolen funds into Bitcoin and fled to the UK in 2017. The victims had argued that British law should apply, as this might allow them to assert property rights over the billions of pounds in crypto assets. However, on Monday, Judge Mark Turner of the London High Court sided with UK authorities, ruling that Chinese law, not British law, should govern the victims’ property claims, since the underlying fraud occurred entirely in China. The judge stated: "The relevant harm occurred in China. The applicants surrendered their funds in China. The alleged fraudulent representations were made in China. The contractual relationships induced thereby were established in China. The direct economic consequences of the misconduct were also borne in China." However, this ruling does not ultimately determine who will own these bitcoins. But it narrows the path for victims to recover these bitcoins and increases the likelihood that the UK Treasury will ultimately retain the seized bitcoins. According to the Financial Times, the victims' lawyers are appealing. The UK Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) stated that upcoming hearings will determine whether any victims can prove ownership of these bitcoins. Across the Atlantic, seized bitcoins have been institutionalized as part of the national balance sheet. In March 2025, the United States established a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, which includes BTC and other tokens seized during law enforcement operations. No single token was purchased with taxpayer funds. According to Arkham Intelligence, wallet addresses associated with the U.S. government hold cryptocurrency valued at $25.8 billion.

extraction.body: A London court has ruled that the UK government’s likelihood of retaining most of the seized bitcoins has increased. The related bitcoins are valued at approximately £3.8 billion ($5 billion), following a report by the Financial Times that the court determined thousands of Chinese fraud victims cannot claim these coins under UK law. This case involves 61,000 bitcoins seized by the London Metropolitan Police during their investigation of Zhimin Qian, who has admitted to defrauding thousands of people in China. Qian operated a large-scale Ponzi scheme through her company, Tianjin Lantian Gerui Electronic Technology, defrauding over 128,000 investors between 2014 and 2017. She then converted billions of dollars in stolen funds into Bitcoin and fled to the UK in 2017. The victims had argued that British law should apply, as this might allow them to assert property rights over the billions of pounds in crypto assets. However, on Monday, Judge Mark Turner of the London High Court sided with UK authorities, ruling that Chinese law, not British law, should govern the victims’ property claims, since the underlying fraud occurred entirely in China. The judge stated: "The relevant harm occurred in China. The applicants surrendered their funds in China. The alleged fraudulent representations were made in China. The contractual relationships induced thereby were established in China. The direct economic consequences of the misconduct were also borne in China." However, this ruling does not ultimately determine who will own these bitcoins. But it narrows the path for victims to recover these bitcoins and increases the likelihood that the UK Treasury will ultimately retain the seized bitcoins. According to the Financial Times, the victims' lawyers are appealing. The UK Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) stated that upcoming hearings will determine whether any victims can prove ownership of these bitcoins. Across the Atlantic, seized bitcoins have been institutionalized as part of the national balance sheet. In March 2025, the United States established a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, which includes BTC and other tokens seized during law enforcement operations. No single token was purchased with taxpayer funds. According to Arkham Intelligence, wallet addresses associated with the U.S. government hold cryptocurrency valued at $25.8 billion.
