extraction.body: Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private. These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator. The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android. Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use. These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android. Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up. “That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.” In the months ahead, the company said that users will be able to share their vibe-coded creations with a network of trusted friends. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child’s T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store. And if the app ever really becomes popular, there will be a way to shift the personal app to one that’s published on the Google Play Store for everyone to try, after completing the trust and safety reviews. Google will also allow users to curate their own lists of games, post questions about games to a new Community Posts section, and join new 48-hour gaming challenges called Sprints, among other gaming-related feature updates. Plus, the Play Store’s built-in AI assistant, Ask Play, is being updated to offer comparisons, allowing users to see the key differences between similar applications. Google Play apps and games will also be more deeply integrated into Gemini’s conversations. The changes are rolling out alongside Google Play’s new support for an age-range feature that allows parents to share their child’s age range, but not their exact birthdate, with developers to get an age-appropriate experience. extraction.body: Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private. These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator. The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android. Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use. These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android. Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up. “That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.” In the months ahead, the company said that users will be able to share their vibe-coded creations with a network of trusted friends. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child’s T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store. And if the app ever really becomes popular, there will be a way to shift the personal app to one that’s published on the Google Play Store for everyone to try, after completing the trust and safety reviews. Google will also allow users to curate their own lists of games, post questions about games to a new Community Posts section, and join new 48-hour gaming challenges called Sprints, among other gaming-related feature updates. Plus, the Play Store’s built-in AI assistant, Ask Play, is being updated to offer comparisons, allowing users to see the key differences between similar applications. Google Play apps and games will also be more deeply integrated into Gemini’s conversations. The changes are rolling out alongside Google Play’s new support for an age-range feature that allows parents to share their child’s age range, but not their exact birthdate, with developers to get an age-appropriate experience. extraction.body: When I was eight, I remember our train to Mumbai ground to a halt with a great noise. When we started moving again, a good eight hours later, someone pointed out a mangled tail, of all things, hanging from a branch close to the tracks. The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs. For a long time, I thought such things only happened in places like rural India, but I learned a few years ago that wildlife and infrastructure do not mix anywhere on the planet. The FAA estimates that wildlife strikes have cost U.S. civil aviation about $272 million a year on average between 1990 and 2025. In France, the rail operator SNCF says wandering animals affect more than 8,000 trains across the country each year and are among its five leading causes of delays. In Brittany, 120 trains hit animals in 2023 alone, disrupting 660 services and causing more than 15,000 minutes of delays. Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure. “I was convinced the answer was not a louder deterrent,” she told TechCrunch. After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation. “We have taught machines to be brilliant, but only inside the environments we engineered for them,” she said. “Cities, factory lines, warehouses. Fixed geometry, known objects. Stepping outside into nature, I saw firsthand how the same machines quickly go blind. Because nature is complex and always alive.” So instead she joined the AI lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm and started working on a system that could change its deterrent responses based on what an animal nearby is doing, and even what kind of animal it is. That work turned into Flox Intelligence , which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15. Flox makes edge devices that process data on-site rather than in the cloud. Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away. Nozkova says the system learns from experience, too, and varies its responses so animals don’t get habituated to repeated signals. The company currently sells battery-operated devices that can be mounted on poles, trees, and other structures. It also offers a software platform that shows clients where the devices are deployed and what’s happening on the ground. The platform can also generate reports for regulatory compliance and for uses like biodiversity monitoring. The longer-term goal is to make the software portable enough to run on machines that work outside, including trains, cars, and drones. Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations. The company sells edge units up front, then charges an annual software and AI subscription after the first year. Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains. Train manufacturer Alstom is one such partner. The company expects to end 2026 with revenue of about $1.5 million, Nozkova said. As unique as Flox’s product and approach are, the startup is not without competition. Robin Radar’s Scarecrow also uses species-specific distress calls to disperse birds and it records the activity, while iCHASE sells a system that detects birds with computer vision and targets them with a moving laser, adjusting its response as needed. Nozkova says her moat is the breadth of the system and the data Flox has collected in the field, which she calls “ground truth on what actually makes a moose or a grizzly bear move safely.” “Physical AI is walking out of the factory and into the messy, alive outdoors,” Nozkova says. “Every machine that operates outside — trains, trucks, drones, tractors, robots — will need to understand nature, and nature intelligence is the next layer of the perception stack. Almost nobody is building it.” The company has raised about $5 million across pre-seed and seed rounds so far, with the seed round led by Unconventional Ventures and Tilia Impact Ventures. Co-investors across the rounds include GENIUS NY, Norrsken, Satgana, and angel investors, Nozkova said. The company is now opening a $10 million Series A, which would mostly go toward growing from about 150 devices to several thousand deployed units and extending the underlying system beyond its current wildlife use cases. He covered North American and European M&A, equity, regulatory news and debt markets at Reuters and Acuris Global, and has also written about travel, tourism, entertainment and books. It was born out of an AI research lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. The company recently relocated its commercial headquarters to the US. Flox Intelligence is an AI-powered wildlife intelligence company that aims to create a world where humans and wildlife coexist. According to the company, it builds autonomous systems deployed on the edge that guide wildlife in real time using AI, bioacoustics, and applied wildlife science. The technology prevents collisions, damage, and disruption across critical infrastructure, including railways, airports, roads, agriculture, and industrial sites, and provides reporting through the Flox Wildlife Platform. The company claims to replace reactive, fragmented deterrents like scarecrows, pyrotechnics, gunshots, and fences with a modern, autonomous layer of prevention and learning at the edge. Every deployment makes the next one smarter, and collectively, these deployments are building one of the world’s largest non-lethal wildlife datasets and windows into how wildlife moves, adapts, and survives alongside human infrastructure. Flox Intelligence mentions that human-wildlife conflict is already a global multi-billion-euro problem. This keeps growing every year as humans take more space, wild animals are pushed closer to urban spaces, and transportation systems get faster, quieter, and harder to avoid. According to the company, existing tools do not scale and lack adaptive learning capabilities. Flox Intelligence claims to be built on a different premise. It is building edge-based physical AI that can operate 24/7 in harsh environments, where decisions have to be made in seconds. The company combines embedded systems, real-time sensing, and applied wildlife science to speak with animals in their own language. “In other words, it turns wildlife communication into actionable intelligence — enabling critical infrastructure to “speak” with wildlife and gently guide them away from high-risk zones before incidents happen,” mentioned Flox Intelligence. The startup’s first commercial product, Edge, is an intelligent wildlife deterrent system built for harsh, real-world environments, engineered for multiple species, extreme weather, remote sites, limited connectivity, and long uptime. It is always on, multi-species, multi-modal, and deployed at the edge. Flox Intelligence has already started shipping Edge pods to the front lines of human-wildlife conflict, including airports dealing with coyotes, deer, and bird strike risks, to rail corridors affected by large wildlife such as moose and bears. It is also helping DOT road networks where deer and bison collisions drive injuries, fatalities, and financial losses. Some other use cases of Edge include ranches and farms balancing predator-healthy ecosystems with livestock protection, and cities and public spaces that witness wildlife movement. The company reports that Edge has logged over 60,000 wildlife events across 27 species, and early deployments show measurable reductions in wildlife presence in high-risk zones. This funding follows Flox Intelligence’s Seed round in July last year. It has expanded its operations across the U.S. and Canada, grown its New York headquarters, and accelerated commercial deployments over the past few months. The fresh capital will be used by the company to accelerate deployments across North America. It will also support growing international demand for Flox Intelligence’s AI-powered wildlife deterrence platform across airports, rail corridors, road networks, and industrial sites. Flox Intelligence reports that it already works with major airports, departments of transportation, infrastructure owners, and mission-driven partners across North America and Europe. Its partners include the U.S. Department of Agriculture, GRR Gerald R. Ford International Airport, WWF, KWS Group, Boliden, and Alstom.

coreStoryFacts.text: Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure.

That work turned into Flox Intelligence , which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15.
Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior.

Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations.
The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs.

After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation.
Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains.

extraction.body: When I was eight, I remember our train to Mumbai ground to a halt with a great noise. When we started moving again, a good eight hours later, someone pointed out a mangled tail, of all things, hanging from a branch close to the tracks. The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs. For a long time, I thought such things only happened in places like rural India, but I learned a few years ago that wildlife and infrastructure do not mix anywhere on the planet. The FAA estimates that wildlife strikes have cost U.S. civil aviation about $272 million a year on average between 1990 and 2025. In France, the rail operator SNCF says wandering animals affect more than 8,000 trains across the country each year and are among its five leading causes of delays. In Brittany, 120 trains hit animals in 2023 alone, disrupting 660 services and causing more than 15,000 minutes of delays. Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure. “I was convinced the answer was not a louder deterrent,” she told TechCrunch. After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation. “We have taught machines to be brilliant, but only inside the environments we engineered for them,” she said. “Cities, factory lines, warehouses. Fixed geometry, known objects. Stepping outside into nature, I saw firsthand how the same machines quickly go blind. Because nature is complex and always alive.” So instead she joined the AI lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm and started working on a system that could change its deterrent responses based on what an animal nearby is doing, and even what kind of animal it is. That work turned into Flox Intelligence , which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15. Flox makes edge devices that process data on-site rather than in the cloud. Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away. Nozkova says the system learns from experience, too, and varies its responses so animals don’t get habituated to repeated signals. The company currently sells battery-operated devices that can be mounted on poles, trees, and other structures. It also offers a software platform that shows clients where the devices are deployed and what’s happening on the ground. The platform can also generate reports for regulatory compliance and for uses like biodiversity monitoring. The longer-term goal is to make the software portable enough to run on machines that work outside, including trains, cars, and drones. Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations. The company sells edge units up front, then charges an annual software and AI subscription after the first year. Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains. Train manufacturer Alstom is one such partner. The company expects to end 2026 with revenue of about $1.5 million, Nozkova said. As unique as Flox’s product and approach are, the startup is not without competition. Robin Radar’s Scarecrow also uses species-specific distress calls to disperse birds and it records the activity, while iCHASE sells a system that detects birds with computer vision and targets them with a moving laser, adjusting its response as needed. Nozkova says her moat is the breadth of the system and the data Flox has collected in the field, which she calls “ground truth on what actually makes a moose or a grizzly bear move safely.” “Physical AI is walking out of the factory and into the messy, alive outdoors,” Nozkova says. “Every machine that operates outside — trains, trucks, drones, tractors, robots — will need to understand nature, and nature intelligence is the next layer of the perception stack. Almost nobody is building it.” The company has raised about $5 million across pre-seed and seed rounds so far, with the seed round led by Unconventional Ventures and Tilia Impact Ventures. Co-investors across the rounds include GENIUS NY, Norrsken, Satgana, and angel investors, Nozkova said. The company is now opening a $10 million Series A, which would mostly go toward growing from about 150 devices to several thousand deployed units and extending the underlying system beyond its current wildlife use cases. sources.title: Sweden's Flox Intelligence raises €2.5 million to become a “digital shepherd” guiding wildlife away from danger - EU-Startups
passages: Flox Intelligence , a wildlife intelligence company building AI systems enabling infrastructure to prevent human-wildlife conflict, today announced a €2.5 million ($3 million) Seed+ round to accelerate deployments across North America.
It is building edge-based physical AI that can operate 24/7 in harsh environments, where decisions have to be made in seconds.
The company combines embedded systems, real-time sensing, and applied wildlife science to speak with animals in their own language.
“For decades, we’ve relied on reactive tools — from scare tactics to fences — that don’t scale, don’t learn, and don’t protect the corridors wildlife depends on.
For so many years, we have been fighting wildlife, but what if we could communicate with them instead?

“Flox Intelligence is building a future where critical infrastructure can proactively prevent conflict, where animal movement is respected and safer, and where people and wildlife can finally coexist.

The technology prevents collisions, damage, and disruption across critical infrastructure, including railways, airports, roads, agriculture, and industrial sites, and provides reporting through the Flox Wildlife Platform.
This keeps growing every year as humans take more space, wild animals are pushed closer to urban spaces, and transportation systems get faster, quieter, and harder to avoid.
Flox Intelligence was founded in 2020 by Nozkova and Tomas Becklin.
It was born out of an AI research lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm.
The company recently relocated its commercial headquarters to the US.
It is also helping DOT road networks where deer and bison collisions drive injuries, fatalities, and financial losses.
Flox Intelligence claims to be built on a different premise.
It has expanded its operations across the U.S. and Canada, grown its New York headquarters, and accelerated commercial deployments over the past few months.
Ford International Airport, WWF, KWS Group, Boliden, and Alstom.

The startup’s first commercial product, Edge, is an intelligent wildlife deterrent system built for harsh, real-world environments, engineered for multiple species, extreme weather, remote sites, limited connectivity, and long uptime.

Every deployment makes the next one smarter, and collectively, these deployments are building one of the world’s largest non-lethal wildlife datasets and windows into how wildlife moves, adapts, and survives alongside human infrastructure.

extraction.body: Flox Intelligence , a wildlife intelligence company building AI systems enabling infrastructure to prevent human-wildlife conflict, today announced a €2.5 million ($3 million) Seed+ round to accelerate deployments across North America. The round was led by Tilia Impact Ventures, with participation from Satgana, GENIUS NY (operated by CenterState CEO), J.O.S.S. and existing investors Unconventional Ventures and Almi Invest. Sara Nozkova , CEO and co-founder of Flox Intelligence, said, “The future of infrastructure safety will include wildlife intelligence by default. “For decades, we’ve relied on reactive tools — from scare tactics to fences — that don’t scale, don’t learn, and don’t protect the corridors wildlife depends on. For so many years, we have been fighting wildlife, but what if we could communicate with them instead? “Flox Intelligence is building a future where critical infrastructure can proactively prevent conflict, where animal movement is respected and safer, and where people and wildlife can finally coexist. Our goal is to make wildlife intelligence a standard layer of modern operations — and to lead that category globally.” Flox Intelligence was founded in 2020 by Nozkova and Tomas Becklin. It was born out of an AI research lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. The company recently relocated its commercial headquarters to the US. Flox Intelligence is an AI-powered wildlife intelligence company that aims to create a world where humans and wildlife coexist. According to the company, it builds autonomous systems deployed on the edge that guide wildlife in real time using AI, bioacoustics, and applied wildlife science. The technology prevents collisions, damage, and disruption across critical infrastructure, including railways, airports, roads, agriculture, and industrial sites, and provides reporting through the Flox Wildlife Platform. The company claims to replace reactive, fragmented deterrents like scarecrows, pyrotechnics, gunshots, and fences with a modern, autonomous layer of prevention and learning at the edge. Every deployment makes the next one smarter, and collectively, these deployments are building one of the world’s largest non-lethal wildlife datasets and windows into how wildlife moves, adapts, and survives alongside human infrastructure. Flox Intelligence mentions that human-wildlife conflict is already a global multi-billion-euro problem. This keeps growing every year as humans take more space, wild animals are pushed closer to urban spaces, and transportation systems get faster, quieter, and harder to avoid. According to the company, existing tools do not scale and lack adaptive learning capabilities. Flox Intelligence claims to be built on a different premise. It is building edge-based physical AI that can operate 24/7 in harsh environments, where decisions have to be made in seconds. The company combines embedded systems, real-time sensing, and applied wildlife science to speak with animals in their own language. “In other words, it turns wildlife communication into actionable intelligence — enabling critical infrastructure to “speak” with wildlife and gently guide them away from high-risk zones before incidents happen,” mentioned Flox Intelligence. The startup’s first commercial product, Edge, is an intelligent wildlife deterrent system built for harsh, real-world environments, engineered for multiple species, extreme weather, remote sites, limited connectivity, and long uptime. It is always on, multi-species, multi-modal, and deployed at the edge. Flox Intelligence has already started shipping Edge pods to the front lines of human-wildlife conflict, including airports dealing with coyotes, deer, and bird strike risks, to rail corridors affected by large wildlife such as moose and bears. It is also helping DOT road networks where deer and bison collisions drive injuries, fatalities, and financial losses. Some other use cases of Edge include ranches and farms balancing predator-healthy ecosystems with livestock protection, and cities and public spaces that witness wildlife movement. The company reports that Edge has logged over 60,000 wildlife events across 27 species, and early deployments show measurable reductions in wildlife presence in high-risk zones. This funding follows Flox Intelligence’s Seed round in July last year. It has expanded its operations across the U.S. and Canada, grown its New York headquarters, and accelerated commercial deployments over the past few months. The fresh capital will be used by the company to accelerate deployments across North America. It will also support growing international demand for Flox Intelligence’s AI-powered wildlife deterrence platform across airports, rail corridors, road networks, and industrial sites. Flox Intelligence reports that it already works with major airports, departments of transportation, infrastructure owners, and mission-driven partners across North America and Europe. Its partners include the U.S. Department of Agriculture, GRR Gerald R. Ford International Airport, WWF, KWS Group, Boliden, and Alstom.

passages: Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security , says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release.

And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams.

Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach.
She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense.
To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices.

Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying.

extraction.body: The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon. Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security , says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said. Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet. Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach. Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense. Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating. That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts. When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway. “In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.” Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying. “We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said. In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools. To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices. It gathers information, including prompts, commands, running processes, permissions, and users’ previous activity, and uses its own “lightweight” models on endpoints to help assess what an agent is trying to do. What stood out is that Pluto’s system can intervene while an agent is working, Bahat said. If an agent tries to gain permissions beyond what a user intended, for example, the system can stop the action or add instructions into the session that prompt the agent to ask for confirmation. “We can inject context back to the session, and this way I can change how the agent is working,” Bahat explained. The startup also takes an unusual approach to finding customers. In April, it launched Plutonium , a free platform that lets anyone check risks associated with publicly available AI skills, connectors, and add-ons. There’s also an MCP scanner and a catalog of verified components. Bahat claims thousands of security professionals use Plutonium and that the community around it has become an important source of feedback and prospective customers. She said 70% of Pluto’s sales pipeline now comes from inbound interest, although she didn’t break down how much of that comes directly through Plutonium. Pluto said it plans to invest the new capital in developing its product, expanding its security research efforts, and growing its presence in the U.S. It has 40 employees in the U.S. and Israel.

sources.title: Pluto Security Raises $42M as AI Creates New Enterprise Risks
passages: Pluto Security just closed a $42 million Series A round led by Jump Capital, TLV Partners, and Ansa Capital as AI agents create unprecedented security headaches for enterprise teams.
Pluto's approach addresses what security teams are calling the "AI blind spot" - the gap between conventional cybersecurity tools and the unique risks posed by autonomous AI systems.

The funding positions Pluto to capture a significant share of what's shaping up to be the next major category in cybersecurity, but success will depend on how quickly they can deliver solutions that actually work in real-world enterprise environments where AI deployment is accelerating faster than security teams can adapt.
This creates what security experts call "dynamic attack surfaces" that change faster than human analysts can track.
The $42 million war chest puts Pluto in position to compete with both established cybersecurity giants and well-funded AI security startups.

The funding comes as companies scramble to protect against AI-powered threats that traditional security tools weren't built to handle, making Pluto's timing particularly strategic in a market where AI security incidents are spiking across major tech companies.
The enterprise security landscape just got a major new player.
Just weeks ago, Apple tightened macOS security controls after identifying "substantial" privacy risks from AI agents, while OpenAI fired three workers for sharing sensitive data with external groups.

extraction.body: Pluto Security just closed a $42 million Series A round led by Jump Capital, TLV Partners, and Ansa Capital as AI agents create unprecedented security headaches for enterprise teams. The funding comes as companies scramble to protect against AI-powered threats that traditional security tools weren't built to handle, making Pluto's timing particularly strategic in a market where AI security incidents are spiking across major tech companies. The enterprise security landscape just got a major new player. Pluto Security announced a $42 million Series A round today, with Jump Capital leading the investment alongside TLV Partners and Ansa Capital. The timing couldn't be more critical - as AI agents proliferate across enterprise environments, they're creating security vulnerabilities that existing tools simply weren't designed to handle. The funding comes at a moment when AI security has become the industry's most pressing concern. Just weeks ago, Apple tightened macOS security controls after identifying "substantial" privacy risks from AI agents, while OpenAI fired three workers for sharing sensitive data with external groups. These incidents highlight how traditional security frameworks are struggling to keep pace with AI-powered threats. Pluto's approach addresses what security teams are calling the "AI blind spot" - the gap between conventional cybersecurity tools and the unique risks posed by autonomous AI systems. While companies rush to deploy AI agents for productivity gains, many are discovering these systems can access sensitive data, make unauthorized API calls, and even interact with external services in ways that bypass traditional security controls. Kevin Mandia's Armadin recently raised $255.5 million at a $2.5 billion valuation for AI security agent swarms, while NVIDIA launched a comprehensive AI agent security platform with full-stack governance capabilities. The competition is heating up, but there's clearly room for multiple players in what analysts predict will be a multi-billion dollar market. What makes Pluto's timing particularly smart is how enterprise security teams are being caught off-guard by AI deployment. Unlike traditional software rollouts that IT teams can control and monitor, AI agents often operate with broad permissions and can evolve their behavior in unexpected ways. This creates what security experts call "dynamic attack surfaces" that change faster than human analysts can track. The $42 million war chest puts Pluto in position to compete with both established cybersecurity giants and well-funded AI security startups. Jump Capital's involvement is particularly noteworthy - the firm has a strong track record in enterprise software and typically leads rounds for companies they believe can scale to billion-dollar valuations. For enterprise CISOs already dealing with Active Directory migration risks and traditional security challenges, AI agents represent a fundamentally new category of risk. They're not just another application to secure - they're autonomous systems that can make decisions, access data, and interact with other systems in ways that traditional security policies never anticipated. The broader trend here is unmistakable: as AI becomes more autonomous and capable, the security implications multiply exponentially. OpenAI's recent review of rogue AI agents following incidents where agents accessed government portals without authorization shows how quickly things can go wrong when AI systems operate beyond their intended boundaries. Pluto Security's $42 million raise reflects a fundamental shift in enterprise security priorities. As AI agents become standard business tools, companies need security solutions built specifically for autonomous systems that can think, learn, and act independently. The funding positions Pluto to capture a significant share of what's shaping up to be the next major category in cybersecurity, but success will depend on how quickly they can deliver solutions that actually work in real-world enterprise environments where AI deployment is accelerating faster than security teams can adapt.

extraction.body: The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon. Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security , says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said. Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet. Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach. Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense. Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating. That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts. When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway. “In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.” Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying. “We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said. In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools. To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices. It gathers information, including prompts, commands, running processes, permissions, and users’ previous activity, and uses its own “lightweight” models on endpoints to help assess what an agent is trying to do. What stood out is that Pluto’s system can intervene while an agent is working, Bahat said. If an agent tries to gain permissions beyond what a user intended, for example, the system can stop the action or add instructions into the session that prompt the agent to ask for confirmation. “We can inject context back to the session, and this way I can change how the agent is working,” Bahat explained. The startup also takes an unusual approach to finding customers. In April, it launched Plutonium , a free platform that lets anyone check risks associated with publicly available AI skills, connectors, and add-ons. There’s also an MCP scanner and a catalog of verified components. Bahat claims thousands of security professionals use Plutonium and that the community around it has become an important source of feedback and prospective customers. She said 70% of Pluto’s sales pipeline now comes from inbound interest, although she didn’t break down how much of that comes directly through Plutonium. Pluto said it plans to invest the new capital in developing its product, expanding its security research efforts, and growing its presence in the U.S. It has 40 employees in the U.S. and Israel.

extraction.body: Pluto Security just closed a $42 million Series A round led by Jump Capital, TLV Partners, and Ansa Capital as AI agents create unprecedented security headaches for enterprise teams. The funding comes as companies scramble to protect against AI-powered threats that traditional security tools weren't built to handle, making Pluto's timing particularly strategic in a market where AI security incidents are spiking across major tech companies. The enterprise security landscape just got a major new player. Pluto Security announced a $42 million Series A round today, with Jump Capital leading the investment alongside TLV Partners and Ansa Capital. The timing couldn't be more critical - as AI agents proliferate across enterprise environments, they're creating security vulnerabilities that existing tools simply weren't designed to handle. The funding comes at a moment when AI security has become the industry's most pressing concern. Just weeks ago, Apple tightened macOS security controls after identifying "substantial" privacy risks from AI agents, while OpenAI fired three workers for sharing sensitive data with external groups. These incidents highlight how traditional security frameworks are struggling to keep pace with AI-powered threats. Pluto's approach addresses what security teams are calling the "AI blind spot" - the gap between conventional cybersecurity tools and the unique risks posed by autonomous AI systems. While companies rush to deploy AI agents for productivity gains, many are discovering these systems can access sensitive data, make unauthorized API calls, and even interact with external services in ways that bypass traditional security controls. Kevin Mandia's Armadin recently raised $255.5 million at a $2.5 billion valuation for AI security agent swarms, while NVIDIA launched a comprehensive AI agent security platform with full-stack governance capabilities. The competition is heating up, but there's clearly room for multiple players in what analysts predict will be a multi-billion dollar market. What makes Pluto's timing particularly smart is how enterprise security teams are being caught off-guard by AI deployment. Unlike traditional software rollouts that IT teams can control and monitor, AI agents often operate with broad permissions and can evolve their behavior in unexpected ways. This creates what security experts call "dynamic attack surfaces" that change faster than human analysts can track. The $42 million war chest puts Pluto in position to compete with both established cybersecurity giants and well-funded AI security startups. Jump Capital's involvement is particularly noteworthy - the firm has a strong track record in enterprise software and typically leads rounds for companies they believe can scale to billion-dollar valuations. For enterprise CISOs already dealing with Active Directory migration risks and traditional security challenges, AI agents represent a fundamentally new category of risk. They're not just another application to secure - they're autonomous systems that can make decisions, access data, and interact with other systems in ways that traditional security policies never anticipated. The broader trend here is unmistakable: as AI becomes more autonomous and capable, the security implications multiply exponentially. OpenAI's recent review of rogue AI agents following incidents where agents accessed government portals without authorization shows how quickly things can go wrong when AI systems operate beyond their intended boundaries. Pluto Security's $42 million raise reflects a fundamental shift in enterprise security priorities. As AI agents become standard business tools, companies need security solutions built specifically for autonomous systems that can think, learn, and act independently. The funding positions Pluto to capture a significant share of what's shaping up to be the next major category in cybersecurity, but success will depend on how quickly they can deliver solutions that actually work in real-world enterprise environments where AI deployment is accelerating faster than security teams can adapt.

As part of a Homeland Security Task Force case, a federal grand jury in Del Rio, Texas, returned an indictment this week charging 11 defendants for their alleged involvement in an attempted alien smuggling operation that resulted in multiple illegal aliens being found dead inside a shipping container in May. According to the indictment, from at least April 2023 through May 12, 2026, the defendants and others operated a human smuggling organization that illegally used cargo trains to smuggle aliens further into the United States after illegally crossing them from Mexico.Each smuggled alien, or their families and friends, paid smugglers in Honduras, Mexico, the United States, and elsewhere between $1,500 and $10,000. The indictment alleges that, toward the end of April 2026, the organization began facilitating the smuggling of at least seven aliens from Acuña, Mexico into Del Rio. On or about May 9, after the smugglers illegally crossed the seven aliens from Mexico into the Del Rio area, the organization transported the aliens to an area near the Union Pacific train tracks in Del Rio. From approximately 1:18 p.m. to 1:25 p.m., while a Union Pacific train was stationary, smugglers, using red bolt cutters, allegedly cut the lock off a Conex shipping container’s door, loaded the aliens into the container, and then shut the door. The shipping container was stacked on top of another and had no ventilation or cooling system. Based on the investigation, the recorded outside temperatures for that day ranged from 88 to 92 degrees Fahrenheit. In total, seven aliens were loaded into the container, including one 14-year-old child. It was secured from the outside and could not be opened from the inside. The train then departed Del Rio and traveled east along U.S. highway 90 to San Antonio. Once the train arrived in San Antonio, smugglers opened the door to the Conex container and discovered the aliens in peril. The smugglers then fled the scene, allegedly leaving one of the deceased aliens near the railroad tracks. Smugglers left the remaining aliens in the shipping container. The next day, the train departed south along its route to Laredo. On May 10, a worker at the Union Pacific Rail Yard in Laredo saw a leg sticking out from a Conex shipping container. Upon inspection, six aliens were discovered deceased in the shipping container. Laredo law enforcement contacted San Antonio agents for assistance. Later, San Antonio law enforcement discovered the seventh alien deceased and abandoned by the railroad tracks in San Antonio. Ultimately, seven aliens died from being in the Conex shipping container—four were Mexican nationals and three were Honduran nationals. One of the aliens was a 14-year-old child. The investigation revealed that at least one alien messaged a loved one, pleading for help. Mayra Alejandra Huerta was arrested May 12 in Del Rio and initially charged with one count of harboring illegal aliens. She has remained in federal custody and now faces two charges in today’s indictment. Last week, eight other defendants were arrested over a multi-day HSTF operation across central and south Texas. Two defendants, Karina Garcia and Seferino Huerta-Casillas, remain at large. All 11 defendants are charged with one count of conspiracy to transport illegal aliens resulting in death and one count of aiding and abetting transport of illegal aliens resulting in death. If convicted, the defendants would each face maximum penalties of life in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas, and Acting Executive Associate Director John A. Condon of Homeland Security Investigations made the announcement. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Sarah Spears, Todd Keagle, and Ashley Ellis-Dotson for the Western District of Texas are prosecuting the case. This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF comprises agents and officers from FBI; ICE HSI; DEA; ATF; U.S. Border Patrol; USMS; U.S. Postal Inspection Service; Department of Transportation; IRS Criminal Investigation; Texas Department of Public Safety; as well as local police departments and sheriff’s offices, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas. An indictment is merely an allegation and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. As part of a Homeland Security Task Force case, a federal grand jury in Del Rio, Texas, returned an indictment this week charging 11 defendants for their alleged involvement in an attempted alien smuggling operation that resulted in multiple illegal aliens being found dead inside a shipping container in May.

According to the indictment, from at least April 2023 through May 12, 2026, the defendants and others operated a human smuggling organization that illegally used cargo trains to smuggle aliens further into the United States after illegally crossing them from Mexico.Each smuggled alien, or their families and friends, paid smugglers in Honduras, Mexico, the United States, and elsewhere between $1,500 and $10,000.

The indictment alleges that, toward the end of April 2026, the organization began facilitating the smuggling of at least seven aliens from Acuña, Mexico into Del Rio. On or about May 9, after the smugglers illegally crossed the seven aliens from Mexico into the Del Rio area, the organization transported the aliens to an area near the Union Pacific train tracks in Del Rio. From approximately 1:18 p.m. to 1:25 p.m., while a Union Pacific train was stationary, smugglers, using red bolt cutters, allegedly cut the lock off a Conex shipping container’s door, loaded the aliens into the container, and then shut the door.

The shipping container was stacked on top of another and had no ventilation or cooling system. Based on the investigation, the recorded outside temperatures for that day ranged from 88 to 92 degrees Fahrenheit. In total, seven aliens were loaded into the container, including one 14-year-old child. It was secured from the outside and could not be opened from the inside. The train then departed Del Rio and traveled east along U.S. highway 90 to San Antonio.

Once the train arrived in San Antonio, smugglers opened the door to the Conex container and discovered the aliens in peril. The smugglers then fled the scene, allegedly leaving one of the deceased aliens near the railroad tracks. Smugglers left the remaining aliens in the shipping container. The next day, the train departed south along its route to Laredo.

On May 10, a worker at the Union Pacific Rail Yard in Laredo saw a leg sticking out from a Conex shipping container. Upon inspection, six aliens were discovered deceased in the shipping container. Laredo law enforcement contacted San Antonio agents for assistance. Later, San Antonio law enforcement discovered the seventh alien deceased and abandoned by the railroad tracks in San Antonio. Ultimately, seven aliens died from being in the Conex shipping container—four were Mexican nationals and three were Honduran nationals. One of the aliens was a 14-year-old child. The investigation revealed that at least one alien messaged a loved one, pleading for help.

Mayra Alejandra Huerta was arrested May 12 in Del Rio and initially charged with one count of harboring illegal aliens. She has remained in federal custody and now faces two charges in today’s indictment. Last week, eight other defendants were arrested over a multi-day HSTF operation across central and south Texas. Two defendants, Karina Garcia and Seferino Huerta-Casillas, remain at large.

All 11 defendants are charged with one count of conspiracy to transport illegal aliens resulting in death and one count of aiding and abetting transport of illegal aliens resulting in death. If convicted, the defendants would each face maximum penalties of life in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas, and Acting Executive Associate Director John A. Condon of Homeland Security Investigations made the announcement.
Assistant U.S. Attorneys Sarah Spears, Todd Keagle, and Ashley Ellis-Dotson for the Western District of Texas are prosecuting the case.

This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF comprises agents and officers from FBI; ICE HSI; DEA; ATF; U.S. Border Patrol; USMS; U.S. Postal Inspection Service; Department of Transportation; IRS Criminal Investigation; Texas Department of Public Safety; as well as local police departments and sheriff’s offices, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas.
An indictment is merely an allegation and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

On October 5, HSI Philadelphia arrested Paulo Jorge Silva, a Lawful Permanent Resident (LPR) from Portugal, in Philadelphia. Silva has been charged with voting by an alien after voting records show that he is an active registered voter in Philadelphia and voted in the November 5, 2024 election. Paulo Jorge Silva (right) during his arrest by HSI Philadelphia Silva was transferred to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS). “This alien from Portugal has been charged with illegally voting in the 2024 election in Pennsylvania,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “When even one non-citizen votes in our elections, it steals the vote of an honest, hard-working American citizen. It’s also AGAINST the law. If we catch an alien illegally voting in our elections, we will hunt you down and arrest you. You’ve been warned. The Trump Administration will always defend the integrity of our election system, and we will make sure that only American citizens are electing American leaders.” Silva was lawfully admitted to the United States through New York in April 1978. The case is being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. An official website of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security

passages: Bitcoin Must Prepare for Quantum Threat Now, Coinbase Says

Coinbase's quantum advisory council is urging blockchain developers to begin preparing for a post-quantum future now, arguing that the technical work of upgrading Bitcoin , Ethereum , and other networks shouldn't wait for consensus on what to do with vulnerable or abandoned coins.

In a new report released Thursday, the council identified one of the most contentious questions facing the industry of what happens to the cryptocurrency whose owners never migrate to quantum-safe addresses.

“No quantum computer can break blockchain cryptography right now,” the council wrote. “But timelines are uncertain, and the crypto community needs to start preparing now rather than debating exactly when the threat will arrive.”

Launched in January, Coinbase's Independent Advisory Board on Quantum Computing and Blockchain brings together researchers from academia and industry, including representatives from Stanford University, the University of Texas at Austin, the Ethereum Foundation, Eigen Labs, Bar-Ilan University, and UC Santa Barbara, to study quantum risks to blockchain networks.

The report comes as researchers warn that a "cryptographically relevant quantum computer"—one powerful enough to crack the elliptic curve digital signatures protecting Bitcoin, Ethereum, and other major blockchains—is more likely than not to exist as early as 2030.

According to the advisory council, the issue could affect millions of Bitcoin sitting in legacy addresses where public keys are already exposed, making them directly vulnerable to a future quantum attack.

“Many of these are believed to be Satoshi's coins or funds whose owners have long since lost their keys,” they wrote. “Factor in address reuse across other address types, and approximately 7 million Bitcoin total are currently considered quantum-vulnerable.”

The report outlines three options for coins that don’t migrate to quantum-safe addresses. First, permanently freeze (or burn) them after a deadline. Second, do nothing and let users decide, adding that “forcing coins to be burned overrides property rights and sets a precedent for network-level interference that conflicts with Bitcoin's core principles.” Third, use middle-ground steps like limiting how many vulnerable coins can move per block or accepting special cryptographic proofs in place of legacy signatures, and let users “pre-commit to migrations without publicly moving funds yet.”
“We stress that the above proposals are compatible with each other; there is no reason to not adopt more than one or all of them, since each has its own advantages,” they wrote.
The debate comes as major blockchain networks begin preparing for a post-quantum future.

In January, the Ethereum Foundation formed a team to coordinate Ethereum's transition to post-quantum security and has explored replacing validator and wallet signatures with quantum-resistant alternatives. This was followed in February by Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin mapping out a quantum upgrade roadmap.

In April, the Coinbase advisory council warned that proof-of-stake networks, including Ethereum and Solana , may be particularly vulnerable to future quantum attacks because the validator signatures used to secure those blockchains rely on cryptography that quantum computers could eventually break.

On Tuesday, the Stellar Development Foundation unveiled a roadmap for migrating users to quantum-safe cryptography. Bitcoin developers, meanwhile, continue to debate how vulnerable coins should be migrated—and what should happen to those that never move.

“The right time to prepare for a cryptographic transition is before it becomes urgent,” a Coinbase Advisory Board spokesperson previously told Decrypt . “Our view is that customer assets are safe today, but the industry should not confuse ‘not imminent’ with ‘not important.’”

passages: The team concludes: “We are grateful to the researchers, developers, and builders already working on these questions, and we look forward to continuing to collaborate with the community on Bitcoin’s post-quantum future.”
Company leaders write: “Some questions, including how to handle abandoned or inaccessible coins, are difficult and deserve thoughtful debate.
In our view, that discussion can continue alongside the technical work to add post-quantum signature support to Bitcoin.”
The company acknowledged that no single solution may satisfy Bitcoin’s technical limits and the needs of every user, custodian and institution.
Its immediate aim is to put those requirements into the discussion while work on quantum-resistant signatures continues.
In a blog post outlining its technical priorities , the cryptocurrency exchange and custodian said protecting Bitcoin will require more than selecting a new digital signature system.
The transition must also work for ordinary wallets and institutional custody, limit demands on the network and address funds whose owners cannot or will not move them.
Coinbase described the migration as a complex, multiyear undertaking.
The Quantum Insider (TQI) is the leading source for the latest quantum technology news, market intelligence, industry analysis, and data covering the global quantum ecosystem.
Coinbase says Bitcoin should begin preparing for quantum computing threats before a machine capable of breaking its cryptography is announced.
The post is an input to an open discussion rather than a final Coinbase position, the company said, ading that it does not establish a migration deadline or announce an agreed Bitcoin upgrade.
Coinbase said evaluations should measure transaction size, fees, verification work and the time required to migrate vulnerable funds.
A system that performs well in a general cryptography test might impose different costs when used across Bitcoin.
Coinbase said developers should consider a route for legitimate users who migrate late if Bitcoin eventually limits or ends spending through existing signatures.
How such a route would work, and what compromises it would require, remain open questions.

It is preparing its own systems, holding discussions with Bitcoin developers and researchers, and supporting open-source work through engineering resources and participation in the Bitcoin Security Consortium.
Coinbase wants Bitcoin developers to evaluate protections for both funds already exposed and newly created funds.
It also wants a design that can accommodate different quantum-resistant signature systems over time, allowing an algorithm to be replaced or supplemented without rebuilding the entire structure.
According to the post, comparisons developed for internet security do not translate directly because Bitcoin signatures are retained permanently and verified by the network’s nodes.

Coinbase called for a reproducible evaluation tailored to Bitcoin, covering established standards, systems still moving through standardization and alternatives based on different security assumptions.
The company pointed to proposals known as P2MR, associated with Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 360, and P2TRv2 as approaches that appear to offer that flexibility.
These concern how Bitcoin records the conditions that must be met to spend funds.

In a blog post outlining its technical priorities , the cryptocurrency exchange and custodian said protecting Bitcoin will require more than selecting a new digital signature system. The transition must also work for ordinary wallets and institutional custody, limit demands on the network and address funds whose owners cannot or will not move them. Coinbase described the migration as a complex, multiyear undertaking. Changes to Bitcoin’s shared rules and the movement of funds across its ecosystem can take years making advance preparation important even before the threat becomes certain, according to the post. The company said it holds about 5% of all bitcoin in existence, giving it a substantial stake in how the network approaches the problem. It is preparing its own systems, holding discussions with Bitcoin developers and researchers, and supporting open-source work through engineering resources and participation in the Bitcoin Security Consortium. The post is an input to an open discussion rather than a final Coinbase position, the company said, ading that it does not establish a migration deadline or announce an agreed Bitcoin upgrade. Coinbase’s main recommendation is to keep technical preparations moving while the community debates what should happen to abandoned or inaccessible coins. Company leaders write: “Some questions, including how to handle abandoned or inaccessible coins, are difficult and deserve thoughtful debate. In our view, that discussion can continue alongside the technical work to add post-quantum signature support to Bitcoin.” Digital signatures authorize bitcoin spending. They allow the network to check that a transaction was approved by the holder of the relevant secret key. The potential threat described by Coinbase is a quantum computer powerful enough to defeat the cryptography behind existing signatures. If that capability emerged, exposed public keys could put funds at risk. Public keys are the information used to verify signatures; private keys provide the authority to spend. Coinbase wants Bitcoin developers to evaluate protections for both funds already exposed and newly created funds. It also wants a design that can accommodate different quantum-resistant signature systems over time, allowing an algorithm to be replaced or supplemented without rebuilding the entire structure. The company pointed to proposals known as P2MR, associated with Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 360, and P2TRv2 as approaches that appear to offer that flexibility. These concern how Bitcoin records the conditions that must be met to spend funds. According to Coinbase , a suitable design would conceal public keys until needed, avoid a spending route vulnerable to quantum attacks and allow future signature algorithms to be added. It would also need an address format that wallets, exchanges and payment tools could adopt with little difficulty. Those protections must fit Bitcoin’s operating constraints. Transaction space is limited, and computers independently checking the blockchain must be able to verify transactions without excessive demands on their resources. Coinbase said evaluations should measure transaction size, fees, verification work and the time required to migrate vulnerable funds. A system that performs well in a general cryptography test might impose different costs when used across Bitcoin. According to the post, comparisons developed for internet security do not translate directly because Bitcoin signatures are retained permanently and verified by the network’s nodes. Coinbase called for a reproducible evaluation tailored to Bitcoin, covering established standards, systems still moving through standardization and alternatives based on different security assumptions. Its proposed evaluation set includes ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and FN-DSA when standardized, along with other credible candidates. These are different approaches to digital signatures intended to resist quantum attacks. For a person managing a wallet, a failed update or an old backup could create that problem. Checking previous blockchain transactions would not necessarily resolve it because a signature or an update might never have reached the blockchain, the company said. For an exchange, the challenge extends to coordinating servers operating independently across different locations. Coinbase said its systems use that arrangement to process signatures quickly and remain available during failures. A stateful signature system could require exclusive access to a key and its associated record during signing. Restoring from backup would also require a reliable way to determine the current signing state. Coinbase therefore wants clear guidance for wallet providers and an option to sign without maintaining state. Institutional custody introduces another requirement. Coinbase said at least one signature option should have promising compatibility with multiparty computation, or MPC, which allows multiple participants to cooperate in signing without placing all signing authority in one location. The company described MPC as an important defense against key theft for organizations facing persistent attacks. It said compatibility should inform the choice of signatures, while emphasizing that it was not asking Bitcoin developers to create a particular MPC protocol. Coinbase favors evaluating ways to let active wallets prepare before the community settles a final policy for existing signatures. One possible arrangement would give the same funds two alternative spending routes, one using an existing signature and another using a quantum-resistant signature. Users could initially rely on the familiar route, with the other available when needed or required. That proposal is a transition mechanism, rather than a requirement that every transaction use both signatures. The company also wants developers to examine quantum-resistant-only options for early adopters, methods that reduce public-key exposure during migration and staged rules for creating and spending funds under older formats. What happens to coins left behind could prove especially difficult. Any rescue mechanism would have to demonstrate that it could withstand quantum attacks and could not be exploited by an attacker who knew only an exposed public key, the company said. Proposals should also explain what happens when an owner has no recoverable secret or misses a rescue deadline. It also wants a design that can accommodate different quantum-resistant signature systems over time, allowing an algorithm to be replaced or supplemented without rebuilding the entire structure.
According to the post, comparisons developed for internet security do not translate directly because Bitcoin signatures are retained permanently and verified by the network’s nodes.

Coinbase called for a reproducible evaluation tailored to Bitcoin, covering established standards, systems still moving through standardization and alternatives based on different security assumptions.
The company pointed to proposals known as P2MR, associated with Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 360, and P2TRv2 as approaches that appear to offer that flexibility.
These concern how Bitcoin records the conditions that must be met to spend funds.
Those protections must fit Bitcoin’s operating constraints.
Transaction space is limited, and computers independently checking the blockchain must be able to verify transactions without excessive demands on their resources.
The company described MPC as an important defense against key theft for organizations facing persistent attacks.
According to Coinbase , a suitable design would conceal public keys until needed, avoid a spending route vulnerable to quantum attacks and allow future signature algorithms to be added.
The potential threat described by Coinbase is a quantum computer powerful enough to defeat the cryptography behind existing signatures.
